0.title: Last Words: The Final Letter of the Apostle Paul
0.overview:
There is a letter that reads like a last will and testament, a soldier’s final dispatch from the front, and a father’s farewell to his son — all at once. Paul writes 2 Timothy from a Roman dungeon, by tradition the Mamertine Prison below the Capitoline Hill, where prisoners awaited execution. He has already stood before Nero’s tribunal; he expects to stand there again, and this time he does not expect to survive. He has been abandoned by most of his colleagues. Demas has gone back to the world. The churches of Asia have turned away. The winter is coming and he has no cloak. Only Luke is with him.

And yet the letter is not a cry of despair but an act of faith. Paul is not finished. He is fighting, praying, thinking, teaching to the last. He writes to Timothy — the son of his heart, the young man he circumcised and took on mission, who is now in Ephesus struggling with false teachers and the creeping temptation to soft-pedal the gospel for the sake of peace — and he writes with the urgency of a man who knows the window is closing. Guard the deposit. Don’t be ashamed. Endure suffering. Preach the word. These are not polite suggestions; they are dying instructions.

The letter is the most personal in the Pauline corpus. More than anywhere else we see Paul the man: Paul who remembers Timothy’s tears and longs to see him, who is comforted by Onesiphorus’s courage, who feels the sting of Alexander’s opposition, who in his final lines sends greetings from people whose names he has not forgotten. The great apostle is a human being who is cold, lonely, and facing death — and whose faith in the Jesus who appears in this letter (“remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead”) is, in the end, the only thing that has not shaken.

Is this really Paul’s last letter? Acts ends with Paul alive in Rome after two years under guard (Acts 28:30). The early church believed he was released, travelled again, and was arrested a second time under Nero, and this letter fits that setting: he has had a first defense (4:16), he expects to die (4:6), and he writes from harsher chains than in Acts. It was probably written around AD 64–67, shortly before his execution.

The letter is addressed to the minister, but it speaks to every Christian who must hold something precious in a world that does not want it. The deposit Paul entrusts to Timothy — the gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen — is the same deposit entrusted to every generation of the church. Guard it. Pass it on. It is worth dying for. Paul’s life proves the claim.

1.title: Guard the Deposit: Courage, the Gospel, and Faithful Examples
1.overview:
These are Paul’s last written words. He is in prison in Rome and expects to die (4:6). He writes to Timothy, his beloved son in the faith, who is gifted, sincere and timid. Paul remembers his tears and the faith of his mother and grandmother, and then presses the charge: rekindle God’s gift, do not be ashamed, and share in suffering by God’s power.

The ground of courage is the gospel itself (vv. 9–10): God saved us by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began, and Christ has abolished death. So Paul can say, “I know whom I have believed.” The chapter ends with a choice of examples: all Asia, which turned away, and Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found Paul and was not ashamed of his chains.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, an apostle by God’s will for the sake of the promise of life in Christ, writes to Timothy, his dear son, with grace, mercy and peace. This is his last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Personal Letter, Not a Church Order

There is no thanksgiving for a congregation because none is in view: this is an old man writing to a younger one while there is still time, and ‘mercy’ appears in the greeting as it does only in the letters to Timothy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul calls himself the Lord's prisoner, not Rome's (v.8; cf. Eph 3:1).

Now: A man facing execution opens his last letter with ‘the promise of the life’: the letter's whole argument in its first sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Timothy 1 is a call not to be ashamed of the gospel, written by a man about to die for it. Paul greets Timothy and recalls the faith of his mother and grandmother (vv. 1–5); urges him to fan into flame God’s gift and to share in suffering (vv. 6–8); sets out the gospel that makes it worth suffering for (vv. 9–12); charges him to guard the good deposit (vv. 13–14); and sets the deserters of Asia beside the loyalty of Onesiphorus (vv. 15–18). A letter written in the shadow of the executioner turns out to be about life.

The setting. This is Paul’s last surviving letter, written from prison in Rome around AD 64–67, probably during Nero’s persecution after the great fire of Rome (AD 64). His first imprisonment (Acts 28) had been a house arrest with freedom to receive visitors; this one was harsher. He was chained like a criminal (1:16; 2:9), hard to find (1:17), largely deserted (1:15; 4:10, 16), and, after a first hearing (4:16), expecting execution; tradition says he was beheaded on the road to Ostia. Timothy was in or near Ephesus, and Paul urged him to come before winter (4:9, 21). These are the apostle’s last written words, and he expected them to be.

An apostle by the will of God. Paul stands on the same ground as always (1 Corinthians 1:1; Galatians 1:1, 15–16). He did not appoint himself, and no church voted him in. Whatever a Roman court decides about him, his appointment came from somewhere a court cannot reach. The man in chains is still the King’s envoy, and the chain changes nothing about who sent him.

The promise of the life. Here is the first surprise of the letter. A man facing execution names his commission in terms of life. “According to” (kata) means in keeping with, and for the sake of: Paul was made an apostle to announce a promise, and the promise is life, found only in union with Christ (John 11:25–26; 1 John 5:11–12). And life here means more than more years. Jesus said that eternal life is to know the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3). It begins the moment a person is joined to Christ, and death interrupts the breathing, not the knowing. It is the whole argument of the letter in its first sentence. Rome can end Paul’s breathing. It cannot touch this life, because it is not his to lose; it is in Christ Jesus, and Christ Jesus has already been raised.

My beloved child. In the first letter Timothy was “my true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2), genuine as against the counterfeits in Ephesus. Here he is my beloved child (agapētō, dearly loved). The polemical edge is gone; these are a dying father’s words.

Grace, mercy, and peace. The same triple blessing as 1 Timothy 1:2: grace for the undeserving, mercy for the suffering, peace for the troubled. Among Paul’s letters, mercy appears in the greetings to Timothy (and in some manuscripts of Titus) but not in the letters to churches, and it is needed even more here than there. Timothy is about to be asked to come to Rome, to a man in chains whom most people have abandoned, and to take up a deposit that has cost its previous holder everything. The Father and Christ Jesus stand together as the one source of these gifts. Paul does not pray to a man for blessing; he names Jesus alongside the Father because Jesus is God.

Why does Paul still call himself an apostle, and are there apostles today? Paul names his office because this letter carries Christ’s authority, not merely an old friend’s advice. An apostle in this sense was one personally commissioned by the risen Christ, a witness of his resurrection (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), sent to lay the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20). Foundations are laid once. That is why Paul is now handing the work on to Timothy and to faithful men who will teach others (2:2), not to new apostles. There are missionaries and church planters today, sometimes loosely called apostolic, but no one now carries Paul’s authority. We hear the apostles today by reading what they wrote, which is why this letter is Scripture and not merely a moving keepsake.

On a Tuesday. When you write or speak to someone younger in the faith, notice how Paul begins: not with instructions but with love, and with the gifts of God. A word of correction lands very differently on someone who has first been told he is beloved.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s last surviving letter, written from prison in Rome as he expected to die, probably in the mid 60s AD under Nero. Timothy was probably still in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–14 — Fan Into Flame, and Guard the Deposit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From thanksgiving for Timothy’s sincere faith, Paul moves to the charge at the heart of the chapter: rekindle the gift, do not be ashamed, share in suffering. He grounds it in one of the richest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament, his own confidence in the One he has believed, and the deposit Timothy must guard by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Deposits, Running Opposite Ways

Paul has entrusted his deposit to God, who is able to guard it (v.12); God has entrusted a deposit to Timothy, who must guard it by the indwelling Spirit (v.14). And behind both stands the grace given in Christ before the ages began, by the Saviour who abolished death (vv.9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The faith came to Timothy through his grandmother and mother (v.5; Acts 16:1), long before any laying on of hands.

Now: To a timid man Paul names what he has been given, power, love and a sound mind (v.7), rather than telling him to feel braver.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As did my ancestors. The verb latreuō means to serve in worship, the word used for the service of God at the tabernacle and temple. And Paul reaches back before his conversion. He does not treat his Jewish inheritance as a false start; the God he worships now is the God of Abraham, Moses and David, the God his forefathers (progonōn) served (Acts 24:14; 26:6–7). The gospel was not a change of deity but the arrival of what that God had promised.

A clear conscience. The word is kathara, clean, pure. Paul is not claiming sinlessness but integrity: his conscience does not accuse him of hypocrisy in his ministry (Acts 23:1; 24:16). The first letter made conscience a recurring test: the aim of the charge is love from a good conscience, and men who reject it make shipwreck of their faith (1 Timothy 1:5, 19). Here Paul quietly claims what he required of others, as a man at the end with nothing outstanding.

Priestly service with a cleansed conscience. Paul puts the temple word and the clean conscience in one sentence, and Hebrews shows why they belong together. The sacrifices of his ancestors could not perfect the conscience of the worshipper, but the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:9, 14), and the verb there is Paul’s verb here. The worship of the forefathers was not cancelled when Christ came; it was completed, because the sacrifice their altars pointed to has now been offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10). Paul serves the God of Abraham as Abraham’s sons always hoped to serve him, through the one offering that finally deals with sin.

Night and day. “Constantly” (adialeiptōs) means without ceasing. In a cell, with the hours empty and day and night blurred together, an old man may well have prayed for his friend at three in the morning. His circumstances have shrunk to a few square yards, and his prayers still reach Ephesus.

Your tears. Somewhere there had been a parting, and Timothy had wept, perhaps at their last farewell; the Ephesian elders had wept the same way on the beach at Miletus (Acts 20:37). Paul treasures the memory and does not call the tears a weakness; Scripture never does (Romans 12:15). The Lord Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty (John 11:35).

I long to see you. “Long” (epipotheō) is to yearn intensely. Not that Timothy may be comforted, but that Paul may be. The man who has told other people to rejoice always, who is facing execution with composure, says openly that there is a joy he does not yet have and that a visit from this young man would supply it. Paul was lonely (4:9–11, 16). Contentment in Paul never meant needing nobody.

How can my conscience be clear when I know what I have done? Paul’s own conscience was clear in the same way yours can be. He had been a blasphemer and a persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13), and his conscience was not clean because he had forgotten that, but because the blood of Christ had answered it (Hebrews 9:14; 10:22). A clear conscience is not a clean record. It means there is nothing between you and God that you are hiding or refusing to deal with: the sins you know of have been confessed, and where possible put right with the people you wronged. If your conscience keeps accusing you of something already confessed, answer it with the cross, not with more penance. If it is accusing you of something you have never dealt with, listen to it, and deal with it today.

Is it wrong for a Christian to feel lonely or to need people? No. Paul, filled with the Spirit and certain of heaven, longs to see a friend and says that seeing him would fill him with joy. God himself said it is not good that the man should be alone (Genesis 2:18), and Jesus wanted his friends near him in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:38). Needing people is not a failure of faith; it is part of being made in the image of a God who is himself a fellowship of love. The danger is not in needing friends but in needing them in place of God. Paul has both: Christ stands by him when everyone else has gone (4:17), and he still asks Timothy to come.

On a Tuesday. Sleepless hours, waiting rooms and long drives are poor places for most things, but good places for prayer; a Roman cell was one. The names of the people you love can be carried there, one by one. And a short message to someone you miss, saying plainly that you miss them, costs little and can mean a great deal. Paul did not think it beneath an apostle to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your sincere faith. “Sincere” (anypokritos) means genuine, without hypocrisy: the word for an actor stands behind it, so this is faith with no pretence in it. It is the same word used of the faith the whole charge aims at in 1 Timothy 1:5. Whatever Timothy’s timidity, Paul has no doubt his faith is the genuine article. A frightened believer and a false believer are two very different things, and Paul knows which Timothy is.

Lois and Eunice. Three generations, named. Acts tells us Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1), which suggests, though Acts does not say so, that the father was not a believer and that the faith in that house came down the female line. The women were probably converted on Paul’s first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6–7). “Dwelt” (enōkēsen) means took up residence, made its home. Faith is not a visitor in a house like that. It lives there.

Faith waiting for its name. Lois and Eunice were very likely devout Jewish women before they heard of Jesus, and their trust in God’s promises had a direction before it had a name. The Scriptures they taught are able to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (3:15). Theirs was the faith of Abraham, who, Jesus said, rejoiced that he would see my day (John 8:56): trust in God’s promise, looking for the one promised. When Paul came to Lystra preaching Jesus crucified and risen, that faith found the one it had been waiting for. Sincere faith is not sincerity about anything at all. It is real trust, with nothing play-acted in it, resting on Christ.

How the faith actually travels. Paul has spent two letters on overseers, deacons, elders, ordination and public teaching, and the man he is entrusting everything to was formed by two women teaching a child at home, long before any of that touched him. Nobody laid hands on Lois. She taught her daughter, who taught her son, and the result is the letter you are reading. From childhood Timothy knew the sacred writings (3:15), and it was not an apostle who taught him.

I am sure. “I am sure” (pepeismai) means I have been persuaded, I am convinced. It is Paul’s own judgement, offered to a man who evidently needed to hear it. Some people require someone else to tell them that what they have is real.

Where Christians differ: are children of believers automatically in the covenant? Paedobaptists (Christians who baptise the infants of believers) see verses like this as evidence that God’s covenant runs on through believing families, as it did in Israel, and so as support for infant baptism. Verdict: This verse shows the great value of believing parents and grandparents, who teach their children the Scriptures from infancy. God often works through families. But faith is not inherited; each person must come to faith personally (John 1:12–13). Timothy was taught as a child and came to believe for himself; Scripture does not record his baptism, but its pattern is that those who believe are then baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12). Baptism belongs to those who profess faith. This is held charitably toward our paedobaptist brothers, who equally insist that each child must come to personal faith.

My children or grandchildren do not believe. What does this verse say to me? It says your teaching is not wasted, and it is not the last word. Lois and Eunice could not give Timothy faith; only God could, and he used their teaching when the gospel came. You cannot convert your children either, and you were never asked to. You are asked to teach them, to pray for them, to live what you say before them, and to keep loving them. Keep the Scriptures in front of them in whatever way they will still receive, even if it is only your life and an occasional honest word. God has brought many prodigals home through seeds planted decades earlier. And if they are adults, leave the outcome with him; your peace does not depend on their response, but on his faithfulness.

I was not raised in a Christian home. Am I behind? No. Timothy had a believing mother and grandmother, but Paul himself was converted as a grown man who had spent years attacking the church, and Titus, a Gentile, and most of the first Christians had no Christian upbringing at all. God has no second-class children. What a Christian home gives is a great mercy and a great responsibility, but it is not a head start in grace. And you can be a Lois. The faith that came to you first can dwell in your house and be handed on from you, and your children may one day thank God for the one who started it.

On a Tuesday. Thank God, by name, for those who taught you the faith, and if they are living, tell them. If there are children in your care, a short passage, a question and a prayer, done often rather than perfectly, is how Lois and Eunice worked.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s father was a Greek; his faith came through his mother’s side.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fan into flame. For this reason: because Timothy’s faith is genuine, and real faith can still burn low. The verb (anazōpyreō) means to rekindle, to stir a fire back into blaze, and it implies embers rather than ashes. Paul does not think the gift has gone out. He thinks it needs air, and the present tense means keep it burning. His fire seems to have burned low, as happens to people long under pressure in a difficult post, and the apostolic response is not rebuke but stirring. The “gift” (charisma) is his gift for ministry, as in 1 Timothy 4:14.

The laying on of my hands. In the first letter the gift came when the council of elders laid their hands on him (1 Timothy 4:14). Both are true, for Paul was among them, but here he presses the personal connection. The old man who commissioned him is about to die, and he wants Timothy to remember whose hands were on his head. The gift came from God; the laying on of hands marked and confirmed it.

A spirit not of fear. This is why the fire had dimmed. The word is not the ordinary term for fear but deilia: cowardice, timidity, the shrinking that stops a man doing what he knows he should. Timothy seems to have been naturally timid (1 Corinthians 16:10). “Spirit” is most likely the Holy Spirit himself, as in verse 14 and Romans 8:15: God gave us the Spirit, and he is not a Spirit of cowardice.

Power and love and self-control. Against timidity, three gifts, and each answers something. Power (dynamis), because the task is beyond him, and it always was; the Spirit gives strength to endure and to speak (Acts 1:8). Love (agapē), because fear makes a man self-protective, and love is the only thing that reliably gets him outside himself; perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18). And self-control (sōphronismos), a sound and disciplined mind, because fear distorts judgement, and a frightened man’s estimate of his situation is seldom accurate. None of the three is a command to try to feel braver. Paul tells a frightened man what he has been given, not what he ought to summon.

The Spirit who rested on Christ. These three gifts were seen first in Jesus. Isaiah promised that the Spirit of the Lord would rest on the coming King, the Spirit of counsel and might (Isaiah 11:2), and the Gospels show it: Jesus returned from the wilderness in the power of the Spirit (Luke 4:14), loved his own to the end (John 13:1), and stood before Caiaphas and Pilate with a clear head and few words. The Spirit given to Timothy is the Spirit who filled Jesus, and whom the exalted Christ has poured out on his people (Acts 2:33). Timothy is not told to become a different man by effort. He is told that the Spirit of the Lord Jesus lives in him.

Can a spiritual gift be lost? Paul tells Timothy to fan it into flame, so a gift can be neglected and dimmed. The gift is the Spirit’s equipping for Timothy’s ministry, recognised when Paul and the elders laid hands on him (1 Timothy 4:14). God does not withdraw it lightly, but it is kept bright by use.

Is fear itself a sin? Paul is speaking of the cowardice that shrinks back from duty and from suffering for Christ, not of every feeling of fear. Many faithful believers feel afraid, and some suffer from anxiety that has bodily causes; that is not condemned here. The Spirit gives power, love and self-control to act faithfully even when we are afraid.

What is my gift, and how do I fan it into flame? Timothy’s gift was for pastoral ministry, but every believer has been given some gift by the Spirit for the good of others (1 Peter 4:10–11; Romans 12:6–8). You usually find it not by introspection but by serving: try the needs in front of you, and listen when mature believers say, you are helped when you do that. Then fan it the way you keep a fire going: use it regularly, feed it with Scripture and prayer, keep away from what smothers it (unconfessed sin, bitterness, sheer busyness), and stay close to others who stir you up. A gift left unused cools, and a gift used in love grows.

Does the laying on of hands pass on spiritual power today? Not in the way the apostles’ hands did. Paul’s hands marked Timothy’s setting apart and were joined with a gift God gave; the apostles had a unique foundational role as witnesses of the risen Christ (Ephesians 2:20), and the sign gifts that accompanied them have ceased with that role. This commentary holds that view, called cessationism, because Scripture ties those signs to the apostles’ founding witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4); many faithful Christians, including Pentecostal and charismatic believers, hold that such gifts continue today, and they too insist that every gift comes from God, not from human hands. Churches today rightly lay hands on those set apart as elders or missionaries, as a public sign of recognition and prayer (Acts 13:3), but the gift comes from God, not from the hands. No one needs a special person to touch them before the Spirit can work in them.

On a Tuesday. What has fear stopped you doing for Christ? Name it: the conversation you keep postponing, the ministry you declined, the truth you softened. Then do what Paul does with fear: set beside it what you have been given. Ask the Spirit for power, love and a clear head, and take one step this week while you are still afraid. Courage is rarely the absence of the feeling; it is obedience with the feeling still there.

For worship. God does not hand his frightened servants a lecture on bravery. He gives them himself. Glory to the God who blows on embers, who does not quench a smouldering wick (Isaiah 42:3), but breathes on it until it burns.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be ashamed. “Ashamed” (epaischynthēs) means embarrassed by, disowning. It is the word that governs this chapter, coming three times (here, v. 12 and v. 16), and shame is the pressure Timothy is under. The first thing he might be ashamed of is the message itself, which in the Roman world meant announcing that a crucified provincial was Lord. Crucifixion was the death chiefly used for slaves and rebels, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23), and under Nero it was dangerous to preach. Jesus had warned against exactly this shame (Mark 8:38), and Paul had refused it all his life (Romans 1:16).

Nor of me his prisoner. Here is the real difficulty. Association with a man awaiting execution is dangerous and humiliating, and verse 15 will say that everyone in Asia has already turned away. And Paul calls himself not Nero’s prisoner but the Lord’s, as in an earlier imprisonment (Ephesians 3:1; 4:1; Philemon 1, 9). The chain is Roman; the ownership is not. He is in chains because of Christ, and under Christ’s sovereign control.

Share in suffering. The verb (synkakopathēson) is a compound, perhaps one Paul coined: suffer evil together with, endure hardship alongside. Paul is not asking Timothy to be brave in his own separate trouble but to come and take a share of this one. Suffering for the gospel is a fellowship, shared with Paul and, beneath that, with Christ (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13).

By the power of God. Not by Timothy’s resolve. Paul has just said God gave a spirit of power (v. 7), and here is where it is spent. The courage being asked for is not a quality Timothy must find in himself; it is a supply he is told to draw on (Colossians 1:11).

In the flow. Therefore ties verse 8 to verse 7: because God has given a Spirit of power, love and self-control, Timothy need not be ashamed. The verse is also the hinge of the chapter. Its two objects of shame are taken up in turn: verses 9–10 show what the testimony about our Lord actually is, verses 11–12 show why the prisoner is not ashamed of it, and verses 15–18 set the people who were ashamed of Paul beside one man who was not. And its call to share in suffering runs on through the whole letter (2:3; 4:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should seek suffering, or that all suffering is for the gospel. It means we should not avoid the suffering that comes from faithfulness to Christ. And where we have been ashamed of him, as every believer has, our standing does not rest on our nerve: Christ confessed the Father without flinching, even before Pilate, and his faithfulness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so the way back is the way Peter came, by confession (1 John 1:9).

What does being ashamed of the gospel look like today? It rarely looks like denying Christ outright. It looks like steering the conversation away when faith comes up at work, letting people assume you agree with them, describing church as a hobby, or keeping a quiet distance from the Christian who has become unpopular for saying what you also believe. It can look like preaching only the parts of the message that are admired, and dropping sin, judgement and the cross. Shame is not the same as tact or wisdom about timing. The test is whether, when it would cost you something, people around you would know that you belong to Jesus and to his people. Underneath, shame is nearly always a question of whose approval we feel we cannot live without. The fear of man lays a snare, but the one who trusts in the Lord is safe (Proverbs 29:25), and the cure is to be more taken with Christ’s welcome than with anyone else’s frown.

What if standing with someone costs me my job or my friends? Then you are in Timothy’s position, and Paul does not pretend the cost is small. He asks it anyway, because Christ is worth it and because you will not bear it alone: it is suffering together, by the power of God. Be wise; do not invite needless trouble, and obey lawful authorities where you can (Romans 13:1). But where the choice is between faithfulness and safety, Jesus has already said what is at stake: whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed (Mark 8:38). And he has also said that no one who has left anything for his sake will fail to receive far more (Mark 10:29–30).

On a Tuesday. Think of one fellow believer who is under pressure or out of favour, and stand next to them this week, publicly, in some small way.

For worship. The Lord Jesus was not ashamed of us. He endured the cross, despising its shame (Hebrews 12:2); he let himself be numbered with criminals and hung where the whole city could see; and he is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The prisoner Paul belongs to him, and so does every believer who has ever been mocked for his name. What we share when we suffer for the gospel is not a lonely heroism but his own fellowship. He was put to shame for us, and he will one day own us before his Father and the holy angels.

verseByVerse.quote: who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who saved us. Paul has asked Timothy to suffer by the power of God, and then, characteristically, cannot mention God without describing him. What follows is one of the densest statements of the gospel in the New Testament, and it has the compression of something already sung. “Saved” (sōsantos) is a past tense: Paul speaks of salvation as something God has already done. Saved from what? From the guilt of sin and the just anger of God against it (Romans 5:9), and from sin’s rule over us (Matthew 1:21). The holy God did not lower his standard to save us; he rescued us from what that standard rightly brings. The power that enables us to suffer is the power that saved us, and salvation is God’s work from first to last.

A holy calling. Both verbs are past and both are God’s. “Called” (kalesantos) is God’s effectual call: the inward work of the Spirit, through the gospel, by which God brings his chosen ones to faith (Romans 8:30; 1 Corinthians 1:9). It is not an invitation that may or may not be accepted but a summons that brings the dead to life, as Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb. A “holy calling” is a calling to be holy, set apart for God (1 Thessalonians 4:7), and a calling that comes from a holy God. So God did not save you and then leave you as you were. The same call that brought you to faith now claims your body, your speech, your money and your time, because God did not call us to impurity but to holiness (1 Thessalonians 4:3–7).

Not because of our works. Paul is emphatic about the order: the negative first. Salvation is not a reward for anything we have done, are doing, or will do (Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 3:5), not even for foreseen works or foreseen faith. “Purpose” (prothesis) is a plan, a resolve, a setting forth beforehand. “His own”: the reason for salvation lies entirely in God, not in us. “Grace” (charis) is undeserved favour.

Before the ages began. Literally, before eternal times (pro chronōn aiōniōn), before time itself. Not planned, not intended: given, in Christ Jesus, before there was any world in which we could exist to receive it. This is election: God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4–5). Whatever else that means, it removes the possibility that anything we have done since is the reason.

Now has been manifested. Verse 10 brings it into history. The eternal purpose stayed hidden until a particular arrival. “Manifested” (phanerōtheisan) is revealed, made visible. “Appearing” (epiphaneia) is the shining-out word, used in that world of a god’s or a king’s public appearance, and used by Paul elsewhere of Christ’s second coming (1 Timothy 6:14). Here it is his first coming. What God planned in eternity he revealed in history, at Bethlehem, at Golgotha, at the empty tomb.

Who abolished death. The verb (katargēsantos) means to render inoperative, to put out of action, to strip of power. And it is past tense, written by a man on death row. Paul does not say death has been made pleasant or that it will one day be dealt with. He says it has already been disarmed. It still occurs; it no longer works. Its sting, which is sin, has been drawn (1 Corinthians 15:54–57), and the one who had the power of death has been destroyed, so that those who all their lives were held in slavery by fear of it are set free (Hebrews 2:14–15). For a man about to be executed, this was not theory.

Life and immortality. The image is of something switched on. “Brought to light” (phōtisantos) is illuminated, revealed clearly. “Immortality” (aphtharsia) is incorruptibility, imperishability: not merely the soul surviving but the whole person beyond the reach of decay. Immortality had been a hope people argued about. Philosophers debated it, mystery cults sold it, tombstones denied it; the Old Testament had glimpses (Job 19:25–27; Daniel 12:2). Paul says it is no longer a matter of speculation, because it has been illuminated by an event. Christ came out of the grave, and the lights came on. “Through the gospel”: the message that announces it is how the light reaches us.

Where Christians differ: is election based on foreseen faith? Arminian Christians (who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted) teach that God chose those whom he foresaw would believe. They hold it out of a real concern for God’s fairness and for human responsibility, and many of them are earnest and fruitful believers. Verdict: This verse rules it out: God saved us not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, given before time began. If election were based on foreseen faith, it would be because of something in us. Faith is the result of God’s choice, not its cause (Acts 13:48; Ephesians 2:8). This is unconditional election, meaning that God’s choice did not depend on any condition he saw in us, and it is the strongest ground of assurance: what God purposed before time, he will not abandon. The questions of fairness and responsibility are real, and the answers below take them up.

Why it is here. Paul writes it to persuade a frightened young man to come and share his suffering. The argument is not be brave. It is: death has been abolished, so what exactly are they threatening you with? Doctrine is not a distraction from courage; it is its fuel. A man who knows that his salvation was settled before the ages and that death has been disarmed can walk into a Roman prison to visit a friend.

If God chose before time began, does it matter whether I preach or pray or believe? Yes, because the God who chose the end also chose the means. He saves through the gospel (v. 10), and people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). Election is the reason evangelism succeeds, not the reason it is unnecessary: Paul says he endures everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation (2:10). And you are commanded to believe and repent; election is never a reason to wait. No one was ever kept out of heaven because he was not chosen while he was wanting to come to Christ. Jesus said, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

Is it fair for God to choose some and not others? Fairness would give each of us what we have earned, and Paul has just said that God saved us not because of our works. If God gave everyone exactly what is fair, no one would be saved. No one is condemned because he was not chosen; people are condemned for the sins they freely love (John 3:19). Election does not keep anyone away from Christ who wants him. It is the reason anyone wants him at all. Paul faced this objection himself and answered it with mercy: God has mercy on whom he wills, and it depends not on human will or effort but on God who has mercy (Romans 9:14–16). The wonder is not that some are passed over, but that any are saved.

How can I know that God chose me? Not by trying to read the secret decree, but by looking at Christ and at what God has done in you. If you trust in Christ, it is because God called you, and those he called he chose and will glorify (Romans 8:30). The evidence is faith in Christ, a love for him and his people, a desire to be holy, and a grief over sin, all of which are the marks of the holy calling in verse 9 (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; 2 Peter 1:10). If you are unsure, do not begin with the question am I elect? Begin with the invitation: come to Christ. Those who come find, afterwards, that they were sought before the ages.

On a Tuesday. When you are anxious about death, your own or that of someone you love, read verses 9 and 10 aloud, slowly, and listen for the tense of every verb: saved, called, gave, manifested, abolished, brought to light. All past. Your standing with God was given before you were born, and you cannot improve on a gift that old.

verseByVerse.quote: for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher, which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Preacher and apostle and teacher. “For which” is the gospel of verses 9–10. Three aspects of Paul’s calling, the same three as 1 Timothy 2:7: preacher (kēryx, herald, who announces the King’s news), apostle (apostolos, the sent one, who represents the one who sent him), and teacher (didaskalos, who explains it). Proclaiming, representing, explaining. And that is why he suffers as he does: not because he has done wrong, but because of the appointment. The suffering is not an interruption of it; it is the consequence of it.

I am not ashamed. There is the word again, now applied to himself. He has told Timothy not to be ashamed of a prisoner; the prisoner is not ashamed either. He is not asking the young man to bear something he is privately embarrassed about.

Whom I have believed. Here is the sentence that has held Christians steady for two thousand years. Not what I have believed: whom. Paul’s confidence at the end of his life does not rest on the soundness of his doctrine, though he has fought for it in every letter. It rests on a person he is acquainted with. “Know” (oida) is settled certainty, and “have believed” (pepisteuka) is a perfect tense: I have trusted and I keep trusting. Doctrine matters enormously, and it is not what you lean on at the end; you lean on the one the doctrine is about.

He is able to guard. “Convinced” (pepeismai) is the same word Paul used of Timothy’s faith (v. 5): I have been persuaded. “Able” (dynatos) is powerful enough. “Guard” (phylaxai) is keep safe, as a sentry keeps a gate. “That day” is the day of Christ’s return and judgement (1:18; 4:8). Not until the trial, or until the executioner, or until things improve. Paul’s horizon runs past his own death without pausing at it.

What is the deposit? The phrase is literally my deposit (tēn parathēkēn mou), the banking word from 1 Timothy 6:20, and it can mean either what Paul has entrusted to Christ (his life, his soul, his salvation) or what Christ has entrusted to Paul (the gospel). Since verse 14 uses the same word for the gospel entrusted to Timothy, it may mean the gospel: Christ will guard his own message. But many take it as Paul’s life committed to Christ: Paul has deposited his soul with Christ, and Christ will keep it safe until the last day. Both are true. Perhaps the breadth is deliberate: his life, his converts, the gospel, all of it, everything a man cannot hold on to himself, lodged with someone who can.

Does this teach that a believer is kept to the end? Paul’s confidence is in God’s power to guard what has been entrusted to him, his life and salvation (some read it as the gospel entrusted to Paul). Arminian Christians hold that a believer must keep himself in the faith and may fail to. Believers must persevere, but it is God who keeps them (John 10:28; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). That is why Paul can face death unashamed. This commentary holds that Reformed teaching, the perseverance of the saints, while honouring Arminian brothers who take Scripture’s warnings with equal seriousness.

What if my faith feels weak? Then this verse is especially for you, because it does not put the weight on the strength of your grip. Paul says he knows whom he has believed and that he is able to guard. A weak hand holding a strong rope is safer than a strong hand holding a thread. Faith saves not because of its size but because of its object; a trembling faith in Christ unites you to Christ as surely as a bold one. Feed it by getting to know him better, in the Gospels and in prayer, since Paul’s confidence came from knowing whom. And when you cannot feel it at all, say what the father said to Jesus: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not send him away.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of the things you cannot keep safe yourself: your children, your health, your future, your reputation, your soul. Then, one by one, place them in his hands in prayer. Not resignation, but a deposit. Then, when you are anxious about one of them later in the week, remind yourself where you left it, and who is guarding it.

For worship. He is able. That is the end of Paul’s argument, and it is enough. The Christ who was entrusted with his people by the Father has never lost one of them (John 6:39; 17:12), and he will not begin with you. He kept Paul to the end, through the sword that early tradition says fell on the road to Ostia, and handed him safely to the Father on the other side. He knows the names of everyone who has ever trusted him and he holds them in a hand from which no one can snatch them (John 10:28). He is the faithful keeper of souls, and he guards what we give him, until that day, and for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pattern of the sound words. “Follow” (eche) is hold, keep. “Pattern” (hypotypōsis) is an outline, a model to work from, the word Paul used of himself as an example of Christ’s patience (1 Timothy 1:16). Timothy is given not Paul’s sentences to repeat verbatim but a fixed shape to keep to; he must not invent new doctrine. “Sound” (hygiainontōn) is the medical word: healthy, health-giving. And “that you have heard from me” is the chain this letter keeps tracing: entrusted to Paul, heard by Timothy, handed on to faithful men who will teach others (2:2). That teaching is now preserved for us in Scripture.

Faith and love. The pattern is not held in a vacuum. Not merely holding correct doctrine coldly, but with faith, trusting it, and love, gentleness toward others. Truth and love belong together (Ephesians 4:15). Doctrine kept without faith and love becomes exactly what the Ephesian teachers had: correct-sounding material producing envy and friction.

Guard the good deposit. “Guard” (phylaxon) is the same command as 1 Timothy 6:20. The “good deposit” (tēn kalēn parathēkēn) is the gospel, the apostolic faith. Parathēkē is the banking term: property left with a trustworthy man, to be returned exactly as received. Not developed, not improved. Returned.

By the Holy Spirit. This clause makes the command bearable. Timothy is timid, Paul is about to die, and everyone in Asia has left; the guarding is done by someone who lives inside the guard. “Dwells” (enoikountos) is the word of verse 5: as faith dwelt in Lois, so the Spirit dwells in believers (Romans 8:9, 11), and he makes possible what human strength cannot do.

The first keeper of the deposit. Before Timothy was told to guard anything, the Son had guarded a deposit of his own. The Father gave him a people and gave him words to speak, and in his prayer before the cross Jesus could say that he had given his disciples the words the Father gave him, and had guarded them, so that not one was lost except the son of destruction (John 17:8, 12). The pattern of sound words is that testimony, handed on through the apostles to Timothy. And the Spirit who helps Timothy guard it is the Spirit Christ sent to bring his words to his disciples’ remembrance (John 14:26). Timothy guards what Christ first guarded, with the help Christ gives.

The architecture of the chapter. Set the two deposits side by side and the shape appears. In verse 12 Paul has entrusted something to God, and God is able to keep it. In verse 14 God has entrusted something to Timothy, and he must keep it, by God’s own Spirit. Both directions, same word, and the strength in both cases comes from the same place.

Isn’t insisting on sound doctrine divisive? Not when it is done the way Paul says, in faith and love. The pattern exists to give health, the way sound food does; it is false teaching that sickens and divides (1 Timothy 6:3–5). Christians may differ charitably on secondary matters, and this commentary tries to show where and how. But the gospel itself, who Christ is and how a sinner is saved, is not ours to adjust, any more than a bank clerk may adjust a deposit left in his care. Love for people is exactly why the truth must be kept: you do not love a sick man by giving him the wrong medicine kindly.

I am not a pastor. How do I guard the deposit? By knowing it, holding it, and handing it on. Know the gospel well enough to tell it plainly and to recognise when it is being bent: learn the Bible, not just verses about it. Hold to it in your own life when it is unpopular. Belong to a church that preaches it and pray for your teachers. Test what you hear, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). And pass it on, to your children, to a younger believer, to a friend at work. Every Christian is a trustee of the gospel for the next person.

For worship. The truth that saves us was not invented by us and cannot be kept by us. Councils have erred and churches have fallen, and still the pattern of sound words has come down to us whole, because the Spirit who inspired it guards it. Blessed be the God who entrusts his treasure to clay jars, and then lives in the jars himself, so that the surpassing power belongs to him and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul sets two examples before Timothy: the many in Asia who turned away from him, and the one man who was not ashamed of his chains.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shame, and the Man Who Refused It

‘Ashamed’ runs through the chapter (vv.8, 12, 16). The turning away of verse 15 was most likely personal desertion of a dangerous prisoner rather than apostasy: a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asia, the scene of Paul's most fruitful work (Acts 19:10), turned away at the end.

Now: Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found a condemned man (v.17), an answer to shame available to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who are in Asia. Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey whose chief city was Ephesus, where Timothy was. Paul spent three years there, longer than anywhere else, teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus until all the residents of the province had heard the word (Acts 19:10). It was perhaps his most fruitful work. And at the end, they turned away from him. “Turned away” (apestraphēsan) is deserted, repudiated.

Phygelus and Hermogenes. Two names, and we know nothing else about them. They appear once in Scripture, and it is here, for this. Perhaps they had been prominent leaders whose desertion was especially painful, men Timothy would otherwise have trusted. Their only memorial is this: they turned away.

What all means. “All” may mean a large number, or possibly those from Asia who had been in Rome and failed to stand by Paul at his trial (4:16). But it is what it felt like from the cell. Under Nero’s persecution, association with a prisoner on a capital charge was dangerous. The turning away is probably not apostasy, abandonment of the faith; it reads as personal desertion. People who had genuinely believed the gospel decided they could not afford to be connected with the prisoner. Which is a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.

The road his Master walked. Paul is not the first to be left by those he had poured his life into. On the night Jesus was arrested, the men he had taught for some three years all left him and fled (Mark 14:50). The servant’s loneliness in Rome has the shape of his Lord’s in Gethsemane. And the likeness runs further, because Paul will tell Timothy what happened at his own hearing: no one came to stand by him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (4:16–17). The Christ who was deserted is the Christ who does not desert. He knows that cell from the inside, and he was in it.

Why tell Timothy this? Because of the letter’s central request. Paul is asking Timothy not to be ashamed of him (v. 8) and to come to him (4:9, 21), and he tells him plainly, before he asks, that everybody else has already declined. He does not conceal how isolated he is or make the invitation look more attractive than it is. He puts the cost on the table and then asks anyway. That is how Jesus called disciples too: count the cost first (Luke 14:28).

Christians have let me down badly. How should I respond? Grieve honestly, as Paul does; he does not pretend it did not hurt. Name what happened truthfully, without inflating it. Then do what he does later in the letter: commit them to God, and pray that it may not be counted against them (4:16). Forgiveness does not mean pretending trust is unchanged, and you may need to be careful with people who have proved unreliable. But do not let their failure define the church for you, or Christ. Paul’s gaze moves straight from the deserters to Onesiphorus, and from both to the Lord who stood by him. And remember that each of us has, at some point, been a Phygelus to someone.

Should we name people who have failed? Rarely, and only for a reason. Paul names Phygelus and Hermogenes not to shame them for sport but to inform Timothy, who would be dealing with these men and needed to know whom he could rely on. That is the test: is naming someone necessary to protect others or the gospel, and is it true? Gossip names people to enjoy their fall. Love names them only when silence would leave someone else exposed.

On a Tuesday. Who is suffering for Christ and feeling abandoned? The missionary whose newsletter you have stopped reading, the believer in prison for his faith, the church member who took an unpopular stand. The Lord who stood by Paul has not turned away from you; do not be the one who turns away. Call, visit, or write.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey whose chief city was Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me— may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household of Onesiphorus. Against the desertion of verse 15, one man, known to us only from these verses and a greeting in chapter 4, and unforgettable. His name means profit-bringer, help-bringer, and he lived up to it. Paul prays for his household; some think Onesiphorus had died, since Paul prays for his household rather than for him, and greets them in 4:19 without him.

He often refreshed me. The verb (anepsyxen) means to refresh, to revive; its root has to do with cooling, like the relief of shade or water in a stifling place. And not once but often. Whatever he brought, food, news, money, conversation, a man in a Roman cell was regularly revived because Onesiphorus kept turning up.

Not ashamed of my chains. There is the chapter’s word for the third time, and here it is answered. Everyone in Asia had been ashamed; this man was not. He is the model for Timothy (v. 8). And Paul specifies the chains rather than the man: it was the visible, humiliating, incriminating fact of the imprisonment that others could not stomach.

He searched for me earnestly. This is the detail that makes the portrait. “Searched earnestly” (spoudaiōs ezētēsen) is sought diligently, eagerly. Rome was a city of perhaps a million people; a prisoner awaiting trial was not listed anywhere convenient, and asking after a man on a capital charge meant drawing official attention to yourself. Paul was hard to find, perhaps in a dungeon. Onesiphorus went round Rome making exactly the enquiries a sensible man would avoid, at risk to himself, until he found him.

Mercy on that day. Paul’s prayer for a man who searched is that he would find, and the echo is probably deliberate. He sought Paul out and found him; may he be sought out and find mercy. “That day” is the day of judgement (v. 12). The double “Lord” may refer to Christ granting mercy from the Father, or is simply emphatic.

A visit the Judge will remember. The day Paul names is the day when Christ sits as judge (4:1, 8), and the Judge has already said what he will remember. I was in prison and you came to me, he will say to his own, and when they ask when, he will answer that what they did for the least of his brothers they did for him (Matthew 25:36–40). Onesiphorus went looking for a chained apostle; without knowing it, he was visiting Christ. That is not mercy earned by visiting: the sheep in the parable are surprised, because they acted as people already blessed by the Father. But not one of his searches through the streets of Rome went unseen.

The service at Ephesus. “Service” (diēkonēsen) is he ministered. The man who refreshed Paul in Rome was not doing something out of character. He had been quietly serving for years, and Timothy had seen it. Faithfulness in a crisis is usually grown in ordinary days.

Where Christians differ: does this verse support prayer for the dead? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse, if Onesiphorus had died, together with 2 Maccabees 12, to support prayers for the dead and the doctrine of purgatory. Verdict: It is not certain that Onesiphorus had died; he may simply have been away from home. Even if he had, Paul’s words are a wish expressing his gratitude, not a prayer to change the condition of a soul. Scripture teaches that at death believers go immediately into the presence of Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43), and that our eternal state is settled at death (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no purgatory, for Christ’s sacrifice has fully paid for the sins of believers (Hebrews 10:14). We should not pray for the dead to be released from punishment, though we may thank God for them. Christians who pray for their dead usually do so out of love, and the love is right; Scripture’s comfort is better still, because a believer who has died needs nothing more.

How do I thank God for a believer who has died? Gladly, and often. Thank God for what he gave you through that person, for the grace that was visible in them, and for the fact that they are now with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). You may speak of them to God with love, and tell him your grief; he is the God of all comfort. What Scripture does not give us is any instruction to pray for their condition to be improved, because for a believer there is nothing left to improve: absent from the body is present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Your prayers are better spent on the family they left behind, as Paul’s first prayer here was for the household.

How can I be an Onesiphorus? Look for the person whom others are avoiding, and go. The prisoner, the patient on a long-stay ward, the elderly saint who no longer gets to church, the pastor under attack, the believer whose name is in the papers. Go more than once, because often is the word. Take something practical, a meal, a book, news, an errand done, and do not be embarrassed to be seen there. And be persistent: if the person is hard to reach, keep asking until you find them. You do not need a gift for preaching or an office in the church. You need a pair of feet and the willingness to be associated with someone in chains.

For worship. Onesiphorus searched a hostile city until he found a man in chains, and in that he looks like his Lord. The Son of God came into a far more hostile world, looking for prisoners, and did not stop until he found them; the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). He was not ashamed of our chains. He took them, and broke them. And on that day, when the prayer of verse 18 is answered for Onesiphorus and for all who have trusted Christ, mercy will be found by people who were first found by mercy.
