They are upsetting the faith of some.<sup>19</sup>But God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."<sup>20</sup>Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable.<sup>21</sup>Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.<sup>22</sup>So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.<sup>23</sup>Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels.<sup>24</sup>And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil,<sup>25</sup>correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth,<sup>26</sup>and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.

3.title: Perilous Times and the God-Breathed Word
3.overview:
The last days, which began with Christ, will bring savage times. Paul’s list of vices is framed by love of self and love of pleasure, and it describes not pagans but religious people with the outline of godliness and none of its power. Like Pharaoh’s magicians, they imitate, and like them they will be exposed.

Against this, Timothy has three anchors: Paul’s example of teaching, life and suffering; the people who taught him from childhood; and the Scriptures themselves. All Scripture is breathed out by God and makes the man of God complete. The answer to savage times is not novelty but the word God has spoken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Godlessness in the Last Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A portrait of the hard times: love turned in on itself, religion kept as an outline without power, and teachers who prey on the vulnerable. Like Pharaoh’s magicians they can imitate the truth for a while, but God sets a limit and their folly is exposed.
verseByVerse.theology:
What ‘the Last Days’ Means

The last days began with Christ (Acts 2:16–17; Hebrews 1:2), and Timothy was living in them. The list's final item puts the whole catalogue inside the church: the outline of godliness kept while its power is denied (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The vices are framed by self-love and pleasure-love (vv. 2, 4) and are mostly relational collapse rather than false doctrine.

Now: Imitation has a ceiling: Pharaoh's magicians could not keep pace for long (v. 9; Exodus 8:18–19).

verseByVerse.quote: But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Timothy 3 contrasts two kinds of people and two kinds of resource. First, a portrait of the false and the godless in the last days (vv. 1–9): people devoted to self, money and pleasure rather than God, with a form of religion but no power, who worm their way into homes and prey on vulnerable people, always learning but never reaching the truth, and opposing it as Pharaoh’s magicians opposed Moses, until their folly is exposed. Second, Timothy’s path (vv. 10–17): he has followed Paul’s teaching, life and sufferings, and seen the Lord rescue him. All who want to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted, while evil people go from bad to worse. So Timothy must continue in what he has learned from those who taught him and from the Scriptures he has known from infancy, which make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ. For all Scripture is breathed out by God and equips the servant of God for every good work. The chapter’s answer to a decaying age is not novelty but Scripture, and behind Scripture, the God who breathes it out.

But understand this. Paul’s consistent pastoral method is to tell people what is coming, so that when it arrives it confirms the teaching rather than contradicting it. He did the same at Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3:4). A Christian who has been told to expect savage times is not destroyed by them; a Christian promised an easy road is.

That in the last days. The last days in the New Testament are not a distant future period. They began with Christ’s coming and the outpouring of the Spirit: Peter says so at Pentecost, quoting Joel (Acts 2:16–17), and Hebrews opens by saying God has spoken to us in these last days by his Son (Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18; 1 Peter 1:20). They are the last days because God’s final word has been spoken in his Son: after Christ comes nothing new, only Christ again, returning. Timothy was living in them. Paul tells him to avoid such people (v. 5), which he could hardly do if they would not exist for two thousand years.

There will come times of difficulty. “Difficulty” (chalepoi) means hard, dangerous, fierce. Its only other New Testament use is of the two demoniacs among the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way (Matthew 8:28): times with teeth in them. And the word for the times means seasons, appointed periods. Even the difficult stretches are not random weather; they recur through the age, intensify toward the end, and belong to a calendar somebody else keeps.

Where Christians differ: are the last days only at the end of history? Some, especially dispensationalists (who see God’s plan unfolding in distinct eras, with a separate future for Israel), place the last days only in a short period just before Christ’s return. Verdict: Scripture treats the whole church age as the last days, beginning at Pentecost. Throughout this age, there will be seasons of great difficulty and godlessness, which may intensify before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3). This is the amillennial view: the present age is a time of gospel advance and of opposition until Christ comes once, visibly, to judge and to renew all things. (Amillennial means reading the thousand years of Revelation 20 as Christ’s present reign rather than a future earthly kingdom.) The reason is that Peter and Hebrews both say the last days have already begun. Many faithful Christians, premillennial and dispensational, read the end-time passages differently, and this commentary honours them as brothers; Paul’s point to Timothy stands whichever way they are read.

So should I expect the world simply to get darker until Christ comes? Expect both darkness and light. Jesus said the wheat and the weeds grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). There will be seasons of fierce godlessness, in some places and times worse than others, and Christians should not be naive about them. But the same age is the age of the gospel running to the nations, and Christ is building his church now. So the right posture is neither panic nor optimism about culture, but steadiness: we were told this would happen, we know who holds the calendar, and the King is coming. Pessimism about the world is never permission for idleness in the gospel.

For worship. The Lord of history is never taken by surprise. He told his church, before the first persecution, what the age would be like, and he has kept every word. Above all the savagery of men sits the Lamb who was slain, holding the scroll of history in his hand and opening its seals one by one (Revelation 5). The seasons of difficulty are his appointed seasons, and they are numbered.
verseByVerse.note: The “last days” began with Christ’s first coming.

verseByVerse.quote: For people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For people will be lovers of self. Eighteen items in three verses (nineteen with v. 5), framed by two of them: lovers of self at the start, and lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God at the end. Everything between is what those two produce. Paul does not begin with atheism or idolatry but with the self turned inward, the reversal of the great commandment to love God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–39). Five of the words are compounds of philos, lover: of self, of money, of pleasure, of God, and, negatively, not lovers of good. It is a list about disordered affection.

Lovers of money. This sin follows immediately, and these letters return to it again and again (1 Timothy 3:3; 6:10). Then the outward pride: “proud” is boasters, braggarts, making empty claims; “arrogant” is haughty, showing themselves above others; “abusive” is literally blasphemers, slanderers toward God and people, whose speech tears others down.

Disobedient to their parents. Then the relational collapse, and this is the heart of the list. Disobedience to parents is the fifth commandment rejected (Romans 1:30). “Ungrateful” is thankless: people who receive and never give thanks. “Unholy” is impious, profane. “Heartless” means without natural affection: the failure of the love that ordinarily binds a family without anyone having to try. And “unappeasable” is a treaty word, literally without libation, refusing the truce: a person with whom no peace can be made, who will not accept an apology.

Slanderous. The word is diaboloi, accusers, the very word for the devil, who is the accuser of the brothers. Then the loss of restraint: unrestrained, untamed, savage, haters of good.

Treacherous, reckless. And finally the betrayals. “Treacherous” is betrayers, the word used of Judas (Luke 6:16). “Reckless” is rash, headlong. “Swollen with conceit” is the word used in the first letter for a man puffed up and blinded by pride (1 Timothy 3:6; 6:4).

Lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God. The list ends as it began, with misdirected love. Pleasure has replaced God. Not that pleasure is evil, for God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), but that it has taken God’s place.

What the list is not. Look at what is missing. There is scarcely anything here about false doctrine, and nothing about persecution from outside. It is a portrait of ordinary human relationships coming apart: families, gratitude, affection, promises, self-restraint. The difficult times will look less dramatic than we imagine, and more recognisable. The list describes a culture, and a kind of religious people (v. 5), and some of its traits can appear in believers too.

No longer for themselves. If the root of the list is love turned inward, the cure cannot be another list. Paul gives it elsewhere: Christ died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised (2 Corinthians 5:15). Self-love is not argued out of a person; it is displaced, when a greater love takes hold of him. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). That is why the gospel, and not moral advice, is the church’s answer to an age of lovers of self. The cross is the one sight in the world that can turn a heart’s love outward again, toward God and toward its neighbour.

Does lovers of self condemn healthy self-regard? Paul condemns the self-absorption that puts self at the centre, not the ordinary care everyone has for himself, which Jesus assumes when he says love your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22:39). The modern call to build up self-esteem can feed the very self-love Paul describes; the gospel gives something better, a secure identity in Christ that frees us to forget ourselves.

I see some of these traits in myself. Am I one of these people? The fact that you are reading the list as a mirror rather than a weapon is a good sign. Every believer still has remnants of these sins: ingratitude, a love of comfort, an unforgiving streak. The people Paul describes are characterised by them, and are content to be; their lives are organised around self, and they do not grieve over it. A Christian is someone who has begun to love God more than self, and who fights what remains, confessing it and asking for change. So do not dismiss the list, and do not despair over it. Take the trait you recognise to Christ, who loved God perfectly in your place and is remaking you in his image.

What if my parents ask me to sin, or are abusive? Disobedience to parents in this list means the contemptuous rebellion that throws off all honour, not refusing to do wrong. We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), parents included, and a child or adult must never take part in sin because a parent demands it. Abuse is never to be tolerated or hidden; it should be reported, and the vulnerable protected. Honouring parents can then take the form of praying for them, speaking respectfully, and caring for them in need as far as is safe, even when obedience is not possible and distance is necessary.

On a Tuesday. Ingratitude is the quietest item on the list and perhaps the commonest. It shows in a meal eaten without thanks, a kindness taken as owed, a day that ends with complaint. Because Christ’s love has reached you first, the cure can begin small: a word of thanks to God for something specific, and to the person who did it, said aloud. A heart that keeps giving thanks finds it harder to stay curved in on itself.

For worship. Here is the opposite of every word in Paul’s list. The Son of God did not love himself at the expense of others; he emptied himself. He did not love money; he had nowhere to lay his head. He was not proud but gentle and lowly; not ungrateful but thanking his Father even on the night he was betrayed; not unappeasable but praying for his executioners; not a traitor but the friend who laid down his life. He loved God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself, perfectly, for us. He was everything this list is not, and he gives himself to people who were everything it is.

verseByVerse.quote: having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power. Avoid such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having the appearance of godliness. This nineteenth item is the one that makes the list terrifying. Everything in verses 2–4 could describe the pagan world, and a reader might have nodded along thinking of Ephesus outside the door. This clause puts the whole catalogue inside the church. The word for appearance is morphōsis: an outline, the outward shape of a thing. These people attend worship, use Christian language, perhaps even teach, and would be offended to be told they were not Christians.

But denying its power. What is missing is power (dynamis), the work of the Spirit that actually changes people. “Denying” is a perfect tense, a settled rejection. These people may recite the creed accurately; what they deny is that godliness does anything, and the denial is in the life, not the mouth (Titus 1:16; Matthew 23:27–28). These letters have said since 1 Timothy 1:5 that teaching is measured by what it produces. The form is attractive because it can be kept without surrender. It gives the comfort and respectability of religion while leaving the self on the throne, a means of managing God rather than bowing to him. That is as possible in a sound church as in a false one.

Godliness has a name. Paul has already told Timothy what true godliness is, and it is a person. Great indeed is the mystery of godliness, he wrote, and then described Christ: manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, taken up in glory (1 Timothy 3:16). The power of godliness is not religious energy; it is the living Christ at work in a person by his Spirit. That is why the form can survive without the power. Take Christ from the centre and the outline of religion stands perfectly well for a while: the services, the vocabulary, even the creed. What it can no longer do is change anybody.

Avoid such people. The verb is present tense: keep turning away. Do not argue them down, do not try to reform them, do not give them a platform; it is the same counsel as 2:16 about irreverent babble. The word needs its limits. Paul is not describing struggling Christians or people whose lives are a mess; the New Testament is full of instruction about bearing with those. He means settled hypocrisy, the outline of godliness kept up deliberately over a life that denies it, and such people are not to be Timothy’s project. Nor are forms of worship bad; the problem is form without power.

How do I know whether my own faith is only an appearance? Ask what it is doing, not only what it says. Is Christ changing anything in you over time: how you treat your family, what you do with money, how you speak about people, what you do when no one is watching? Do you pray when there is no audience? Do you grieve over your sin, or only over being caught? Power here is not spectacular experience; it is the quiet, real work of the Spirit making you more like Christ. If you find mostly form, do not try harder at the form. Go to Christ himself, confess the emptiness, and ask him for the life only he gives. He does not turn away those who come. And the very fact that you are asking, wanting to be real, is a sign of the Spirit at work: the people Paul describes are untroubled by the question.

Does avoid such people mean cutting off family members who are like this? Not in the sense of abandoning ordinary duties. Paul is speaking chiefly about religious influence in the church: do not follow them, do not give them a platform, do not let them shape you. You still owe family members love, honesty, and, where it is safe, ordinary kindness, and you may long and pray for their conversion. But you need not let a hypocritical relative set the spiritual direction of your home, teach your children, or draw you into his ways. Where there is manipulation or abuse, appropriate distance is right.

On a Tuesday. The power of godliness is the Spirit who raised Jesus, and he lives in every believer. Ask him to make it real in one area this week, your speech at home perhaps, and watch for the change. It will be real but never perfect, and it need not be: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, and for his sake God gladly accepts your halting obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: For among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women, burdened with sins and led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who creep into households. Paul now says what these people actually do, and it is predatory. The verb means to worm in, to slip in unnoticed: entry by stealth rather than invitation. The target is households, which is where the churches met and where many women of that world spent most of their days. A man with religious credentials could get into a home in a way he could never get into a public gathering, and there he could work without oversight.

And capture weak women. “Capture” is a war word, to take captive, the picture of 2:26, where people are caught alive in the devil’s snare. “Weak women” is a diminutive, little women, with a note of contempt. The scorn is not aimed at women as such. This is the man who named Lois and Eunice as the source of Timothy’s faith (1:5) and lists women as fellow workers wherever he goes (Romans 16:1–7; Philippians 4:3). He is describing particular women, perhaps wealthy and with time on their hands (1 Timothy 5:13), who had become easy targets; what follows describes vulnerability rather than stupidity.

Burdened with sins. That is the profile of the target, and it is the profile predators have always looked for. “Burdened” is heaped up, loaded down, as with a pile: someone carrying guilt, and led along by desires pulling in several directions at once, perhaps for spiritual novelty, acceptance, or feelings. A person weighed down by things they have done and cannot resolve will listen to anybody who offers relief, true or false.

Always learning. These women are not idle; they attend every new class and hear every new idea, but never come to full knowledge (epignōsis). The teaching they are fed is the endless kind Paul described in the first letter, speculation that never lands (1 Timothy 1:4). Learning that never arrives is not a failure of effort; it is what a certain kind of teaching is designed to produce, because a person who arrives no longer needs the teacher.

The truth they never reached. The knowledge of the truth these women never arrived at is not an endless syllabus. It has a destination, and the destination is a person. Jesus said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6), and Paul speaks of learning Christ, as the truth is in Jesus (Ephesians 4:20–21). That is why the predators’ teaching could never let them arrive. To arrive would have meant meeting Christ, laying the heaped-up load of sin on the one who bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). Learning that never reaches Jesus is not a slow road to the truth. It is a road around it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are more easily deceived than men in general. Paul is describing particular women in Ephesus, and the false teachers who preyed on them were men. Nor does it make continued learning bad (2 Peter 3:18).

How do I protect myself and others from teachers like this? Watch for the marks Paul gives: entry by stealth rather than through the church’s proper oversight; a focus on the guilty and lonely; teaching that keeps you dependent rather than settled; and novelty that never brings you to repentance and faith in Christ. Today they creep into homes through screens as well as doors: the online teacher who offers secret insight, the course that never ends, the counsellor who isolates you from your church. Keep your spiritual life connected to a local church and its elders. Bring burdens of guilt to Christ, who lifts them freely, so that no one can trade on them. And if someone vulnerable is being drawn in, go to them gently, and tell your elders.

I keep learning but never feel settled. What should I do? Ask whether your learning is aimed at obeying. Settled knowledge of the truth comes not from hearing more ideas but from submitting to what God has plainly said, and the plain things are enough to begin with: who Christ is, what he has done, what he commands. Narrow your diet for a season: one good church, one book of the Bible read slowly, one sound book on the gospel, and stop sampling. Act on what you know. And settle the main thing first: have you come to Christ in repentance and faith? People who are always learning are sometimes avoiding the one step that would end the search.

For worship. False teachers creep into houses to take captives; Christ came openly to proclaim liberty to the captives, in the synagogue of his own town (Luke 4:18). He never traded on anyone’s guilt. A woman bent double for eighteen years he called a daughter of Abraham, and loosed her, and she stood up straight and glorified God (Luke 13:11–16). Here is a Shepherd who lifts the heaviest load off the weakest back.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith. But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. The names are not in the Old Testament. Jewish tradition gave them to Pharaoh’s magicians, who imitated Moses’ signs by their secret arts (Exodus 7:11, 22; 8:7), and the names appear in Jewish writings and even in some pagan sources. Paul is using a tradition his readers knew, as he uses Greek poets elsewhere (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12), without necessarily endorsing everything it contained. And the choice of comparison is exact. The Egyptian magicians did not deny Moses or argue with him. They reproduced what he did. Their opposition was imitation, which is precisely the danger of men who have the outline of godliness (v. 5).

So these men also oppose the truth. Like the magicians, they resist by offering counterfeits. “Corrupted” is thoroughly rotted, as in 1 Timothy 6:5. “Disqualified” is adokimoi, the assayer’s word again, this time in the negative: metal tested and rejected, counterfeit (Titus 1:16). Timothy is to present himself approved (2:15); these men are the failed assay, and the two verses are meant to be read against each other.

But they will not get very far. Then the limit, and it is the mercy in the passage. In 2:16 they progress in ungodliness; here, there is a ceiling. God will not let them advance indefinitely. That is a genuine encouragement to a man watching a church being damaged. Paul does not promise the trouble will be brief or painless: Hymenaeus, probably the same man disciplined in the first letter (1 Timothy 1:20), was still at work in chapter 2 (2:17).

For their folly will be plain to all. This kind of thing exposes itself in the end, and the exposure comes from the folly’s own nature rather than from anyone’s campaign against it. Egypt’s magicians kept pace with Moses through the first two plagues, and then could not produce gnats, and had to tell Pharaoh, this is the finger of God (Exodus 8:18–19). In the end they could not even stand before Moses because of the boils (Exodus 9:11). Imitation runs out, usually sooner than the people watching fear.

The finger of God. The magicians’ confession, this is the finger of God, has an echo in the Gospels. When Jesus was accused of casting out demons by Satan’s power, he answered that if it is by the finger of God that he cast them out, then the kingdom of God had come upon them (Luke 11:20). He is the greater Moses (Hebrews 3:3), and his works cannot be copied: the magicians could imitate a plague, but no one could imitate the man who cast out demons with a word and came back from the dead. The counterfeits of Timothy’s day, and of ours, can reproduce the outline of his works for a time. They cannot reproduce him, and sooner or later the difference shows.

Why does God let false teachers succeed for a time? Scripture gives several reasons. Such things test and reveal who is genuine: there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognised (1 Corinthians 11:19). They drive the church to understand the truth more clearly; many of the great creeds were written in answer to error. They teach believers to depend on God’s word rather than on impressive people. And they give time for repentance, even to the false teachers themselves (2:25). None of this makes error good. But God is sovereign over it, and he sets its limit. They will not get very far.

On a Tuesday. When some false teaching seems to be sweeping all before it, do not panic and do not join it. Ask of any impressive ministry not whether it can do what the real thing does, but whether it leads people to Christ crucified and to holy lives.
verseByVerse.note: Jannes and Jambres are not named in Exodus; Jewish tradition gave these names to Pharaoh’s magicians.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Scripture and the Man of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against the imitators, Timothy has seen the real thing in Paul, through stones and scars, and the Lord’s rescues. Persecution is the normal lot of the godly. So Timothy is to stay where he is, held by those who taught him and by the Scriptures, which God has breathed out and which are enough for every good work.
verseByVerse.theology:
Breathed Out by God

Scripture is God-breathed (v. 16): it proceeds from him, not by dictation, for its writers genuinely spoke as they were carried along (2 Peter 1:21). It teaches, reproves, corrects and trains, so that the man of God is complete.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Antioch, Iconium and Lystra (v. 11) were the towns of the first journey, and Lystra was Timothy's home (Acts 14:19; 16:1).

Now: Opposition for godliness (v. 12) is not evidence of failure; it is what the text says to expect.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra—which persecutions I endured; yet from them all the Lord rescued me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You, however, have followed. The pronoun is emphatic and turns the chapter. Against the imitators who have the shape of godliness, one young man who has had the real thing in front of him for years. “Followed” is followed closely, observed carefully, as in 1 Timothy 4:6: the word for a disciple keeping pace with a teacher. Timothy had not merely heard about Paul but lived alongside him.

My teaching, my conduct. Doctrine comes first; then everything else is life. “Aim in life” is purpose, the thing a man is actually for; Paul’s was to know Christ and make him known (Philippians 3:10, 14). “Patience” is long-suffering with people; “steadfastness” is endurance under circumstances. One item of doctrine and eight of character and circumstance: Timothy learned Paul not chiefly in a lecture but on the road, watching how he behaved, what he aimed at, and how he took it when things went wrong.

At Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra. These are the towns of the first missionary journey (Acts 13:50; 14:1–6, 19), and Lystra was Timothy’s home town (Acts 16:1). At Antioch Paul was driven out; at Iconium they tried to stone him; at Lystra they succeeded, and dragged him out of the city supposing he was dead (Acts 14:19). Timothy may well have seen it: a man stoned and left for dead, who got up and went back into the city. He knew from the beginning that following Christ meant suffering, and Paul tells him to remember it now that the price has come due again.

From them all the Lord rescued me. The Lord brought Paul through each one, sometimes by escape, sometimes by healing, always by his presence (2 Corinthians 1:10; Psalm 34:19). And this is written from a cell by a man who knows he will not be rescued this time, and he says it anyway, because it is true. That God does not always rescue does not mean he never does, and Paul will say in the next chapter that the Lord will bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom (4:18). The rescue is not cancelled by the execution; it is completed by it.

The Rescuer who was not rescued. The Lord who brought Paul out of Antioch, Iconium and Lystra had himself refused a rescue. In Gethsemane he said he could ask his Father for more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), and he did not ask. At the cross the mockers said, He saved others; he cannot save himself (Matthew 27:42). They were right in a way they did not understand: he would not save himself, because he was saving others. Every rescue Paul lists was bought by that refusal, and so is the last one, through the sword and into the heavenly kingdom.

God did not rescue someone I love from illness or death. Did he fail them? No. He did not fail Paul either, though the sword fell. God’s rescue sometimes comes as escape and sometimes as strength to endure, and for every believer it comes finally as deliverance through death into his presence, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). That does not make the loss less painful, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend it is; Jesus wept at a grave. But it means the story is not over. The believer you lost has been rescued in the fullest sense, safely brought into the heavenly kingdom, beyond the reach of any further harm. He who did not spare his own Son did not abandon them.

Whom should I follow? Look for what Timothy saw in Paul: sound teaching joined to a life that matches it, observed over time and in hardship. Not the most famous person you can find online, but believers near enough to watch: how they treat their families, handle money, endure suffering, and speak about others. Elders in your church should be such people (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Hebrews 13:7). Follow them as they follow Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), not uncritically, and never in place of Christ. And remember someone may be watching you in the same way.

On a Tuesday. Most of us have a Lystra somewhere behind us: a diagnosis that was not what we feared, a debt that was met, a dark year that ended. Remembering them is not nostalgia but evidence, the same evidence Paul offers Timothy.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, where Paul was stoned and left for dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who desire to live a godly life. The sentence is flat and unqualified. Not some, not those in hostile places, not just apostles: all. And note the phrasing: those who desire, want, are determined, to live with reverence for God. The trigger is not achievement but intention. It is the wanting that draws fire, which means nobody can escape by concluding they are not godly enough to qualify.

Will be persecuted. The word is hunted, pursued, harassed. A promise, not a possibility: opposition from a world that hates the light (John 15:18–20; 1 Peter 4:12–14; Matthew 5:10–12). It must be read honestly rather than dramatically. Most Christians in comfortable countries will not be imprisoned, and pretending otherwise cheapens the word for those who are. But persecution runs from ridicule and exclusion to loss of work, prison and death, and its ordinary form is familiar: the family that finds you embarrassing, the promotion your convictions cost you, the friendships that quietly cool.

Persecuted in Christ. The words in Christ Jesus explain why the promise is so certain. The godliness that draws fire is not a personal style; it is Christ’s own life showing in his people, and the hostility it meets is hostility to him. Paul learned that on the Damascus road, from the other side. He was hunting Christians, and the voice from heaven asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The man who now writes that all will be persecuted had once been the persecutor, and he knew whom he had really been striking. Every believer who suffers for godliness suffers in union with the Lord who suffered first and counts the blows as his own.

Have I done something wrong? The verse also settles a question people ask when things go badly. Opposition for godliness is not evidence of failure. It is what the text says to expect.

From bad to worse. Then the parallel movement. “Impostors” first meant sorcerers or enchanters, and by Paul’s day it was a common word for swindlers and charlatans; the magical overtone reaches back to Jannes and Jambres in verse 8. They progress too, but to the worse: the ironic progress again.

Deceiving and being deceived. Both at once, and the order matters. The deceiver is himself deceived, and the two feed each other: a man who tells people what is not true for long enough stops being able to tell (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11). It is a frightening observation, because the state Paul is describing is not one its occupant can detect from inside. But it holds a comfort for the anxious too: a believer who fears being deceived and goes to Scripture to be corrected is not in that state, for the self-deceived do not ask.

In the flow. Verse 12 widens Paul’s own story in verse 11 into a rule for every believer, and so gathers up the call of the whole letter to share in suffering (1:8; 2:3), which comes again in 4:5. Verse 13 then tells the opposite story: the impostors make progress too, but downward. Two kinds of people are moving in two directions, and verses 14–17 tell Timothy what to hold on to while they do: what he has learned, and the Scriptures God has breathed out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution is proof of godliness; some suffer for their own wrongdoing (1 Peter 4:15). Nor does it mean Christians should seek persecution or be needlessly offensive.

I am not persecuted at all. Does that mean I am not living a godly life? Not necessarily, but it is worth asking honestly. God gives seasons of peace (Acts 9:31), and some believers live in places and roles where opposition is light. Persecution is also often quiet, and you may be experiencing more of it than you name. But if your faith never costs you anything at all, ask whether anyone around you knows you are a Christian, and whether you ever take a stand that would be unpopular. The aim is not to provoke opposition; it is to be so plainly Christ’s that, when opposition comes, it finds you on his side.

How should I respond when I am opposed for my faith? As Jesus taught: do not retaliate, but bless those who curse you and pray for those who mistreat you (Luke 6:27–28). Examine yourself first, to be sure it is for righteousness and not for rudeness (1 Peter 3:15–17; 4:15). Rejoice, strange as it sounds, because you share in Christ’s sufferings and great is your reward in heaven (Matthew 5:11–12). Tell your church and let them carry it with you. Use lawful protections where you have them, as Paul appealed to Caesar. And keep doing good: the best answer to slander is a life that makes it implausible (1 Peter 2:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for you, continue. The contrast again, the second time in this chapter (vv. 10, 14), and now the instruction: remain, abide, stay put. Against a world going from bad to worse, Timothy is not told to innovate or to devise a strategy. He is told to stay where he is, in the truth, and the Holy Spirit who dwells within us is the one who keeps him there (1:14). The false teachers progress to worse; Timothy must remain. And he has not merely heard the truth; he has been persuaded of it.

Knowing from whom you learned it. Two reasons follow, the two grounds on which anyone holds the faith. The first is personal. The pronoun is plural in the best manuscripts (some later ones, followed by the KJV, have the singular, of whom): from what persons, Paul and also Lois and Eunice (1:5). Timothy can weigh the teaching against the people it came through; he watched them and knows what it made of them, unlike the false teachers, whose lives discredited their words. That is an argument not from authority but from evidence. When doctrine is under pressure, part of what steadies a person is the memory of believers whose lives could not be explained any other way.

From childhood. The second reason is the text itself. The word for childhood means infancy: from the cradle. The “sacred writings” are the Old Testament Scriptures. Timothy’s father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), so the teaching came from his mother and grandmother. Here the chapter’s threads meet. Two women taught a small boy the Scriptures, and years later Paul points to it as the reason he will hold when everyone else defects.

Which are able to make you wise for salvation. The Scriptures have power; they do not merely inform, they lead to salvation. Wisdom here is the knowledge of God that saves.

Through faith in Christ Jesus. Note the qualifier. The Old Testament points to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44; John 5:39), and its wisdom for salvation comes through faith in him. Scripture does not save by being read; it makes wise unto salvation by pointing to someone. Take the pointing away and you have a man who knows the sacred writings very well and is not saved by them, which describes a good many of Paul’s opponents. A veil lies over the heart until one turns to the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:14–16).

How does the Old Testament make anyone wise for salvation through Christ? By showing us who God is, what sin is, and what he promised to do about it, and then pointing forward to the one who would do it. The sacrifices taught that sin must be paid for by a substitute; the Passover lamb, the scapegoat and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 showed what kind of substitute. The kings of David’s line pointed to the King. The law showed that we cannot save ourselves. Timothy, raised on these Scriptures, was ready to recognise Jesus when Paul preached him, because he had been taught what to look for. That is still how the Old Testament works: read it as the long promise, and Christ as the yes to every promise.

I was not taught the Scriptures as a child, or my teachers failed me. What then? You can begin now, and the Scriptures are just as able to make you wise at forty as at four. The power is in God’s word, not in the age of the reader. If the people who taught you later turned out to be hypocrites, that is painful, but Paul’s second reason stands on its own: the Scriptures themselves, read with faith in Christ. Find faithful believers now whose lives you can watch, and let them help you. And if you have children or grandchildren, you can give them what you were not given. Many a family’s line of faith begins with one person who started late.

On a Tuesday. A bedtime Bible story can look like a small thing. Lois and Eunice probably thought so too, and it held a man steady when an empire turned against him. Somewhere behind your own faith stands a person whose life made the gospel believable to you; a word of thanks to them, if they are still living, may mean more than you know.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Scripture. Every part of Scripture, not just some parts. Not the parts that move you, not the parts a modern reader finds congenial: the genealogies, the building specifications, the imprecatory psalms too. Paul’s immediate reference is the Old Testament, the sacred writings of verse 15, and that should be stressed, because it is the part of the Bible Christians most often quietly shelve.

Is breathed out by God. The word is theopneustos, God-breathed, a single word that occurs nowhere else in the Greek Bible and is very rare anywhere in Greek; Paul may even have coined it. And note the direction: not God-inbreathed, as though he blew life into documents that already existed, but God-outbreathed. Scripture proceeds from him the way breath proceeds from a speaker (Psalm 33:6; Matthew 4:4). The older translation inspired has drifted and now suggests a heightened human state; we call a poem or a performance inspired. That is not the claim. The claim is about origin. God is its source. What Scripture says, God says.

Not dictation. And it does not mean dictation. Luke researched (Luke 1:3), Paul argues and sometimes writes in hot anger (Galatians 5:12), David bleeds all over the Psalms. The writers’ personalities, vocabularies and circumstances are everywhere in the text. Peter puts both halves together: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:20–21). Genuinely speaking, genuinely carried, so that what they wrote is exactly what God intended.

The Lord who trusted every word. The strongest reason for receiving Scripture as God-breathed is that the Son of God received it so. Jesus treated the Old Testament as his Father’s voice. Scripture cannot be broken, he said (John 10:35); he met temptation with it, went to the cross in obedience to it, and said that everything written about him must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). He also promised that the Spirit would guide his apostles into all the truth (John 16:13), which is how the New Testament came to stand beside the Old. To receive the Bible as God’s word is not to rank a book above Christ. It is to share Christ’s own view of it, and to hear in every part the God who speaks of him.

Profitable for teaching. Because it is from God, it is useful. Then the purpose, four uses in two pairs. Teaching: it shows what to believe, what is true. “Reproof” is conviction, exposing error: it shows where we have gone wrong in belief or life. “Correction” means setting upright again: it not only exposes error but restores us to the right path.

And for training in righteousness. “Training” (paideia) is the word for raising a child: the long formation of somebody over years. So the four uses are what is right (teaching), what is not right (reproof), how to get right (correction), and how to stay right (training). Scripture tells you the truth, shows you where you are wrong, puts you back on your feet, and then trains you. It does not stop at diagnosis. A reader who only ever feels rebuked by the Bible is using half of it.

That the man of God may be complete. The title was given to Moses and the prophets, and is used of Timothy in 1 Timothy 6:11: Timothy as a minister, and by extension every believer who belongs to God. “Complete” is capable, fully fit for purpose.

Equipped for every good work. The word is fully fitted out, like a ship supplied for a voyage, or a workman furnished with tools. There is no task God calls us to for which Scripture does not equip us. This is the sufficiency of Scripture.

The answer to the whole chapter. Savage times, imitators with the outline of godliness, predators in households, deceivers going from bad to worse, and what Timothy is handed against all of it is a book. Not a technique, not a strategy, not secret knowledge. Paul’s last substantial word to his successor is that the Scriptures are sufficient to make a man complete and furnish him for everything he will be asked to do.

Does All Scripture include the New Testament? Paul’s immediate reference is the Old Testament Scriptures Timothy knew from childhood (v. 15). But the New Testament itself treats the apostles’ writings as Scripture: Peter puts Paul’s letters with the other Scriptures (2 Peter 3:16), and Paul quotes a saying of Jesus, the one found in Luke 10:7, as Scripture (1 Timothy 5:18). The same breath of God stands behind both Testaments.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture alone the final authority? Roman Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that Scripture and tradition together, interpreted by the church, are the rule of faith. Liberal Protestantism (which reads the Bible chiefly as a record of human religious experience) holds that Scripture contains God’s word but also human error. Some charismatics look for ongoing revelation alongside Scripture. Verdict: Because all Scripture is God-breathed, it is entirely true and without error in all it affirms (inerrancy), for God cannot lie (Titus 1:2; John 17:17). Because it equips the believer for every good work, it is sufficient: we need no further revelation or tradition of equal authority to know what to believe and how to live. Scripture alone is the supreme and final authority for faith and practice (sola Scriptura). Tradition, creeds and teachers are valuable servants, but they must be tested by Scripture and corrected by it (Acts 17:11). And the canon is closed: the apostolic deposit is complete (Jude 3; Hebrews 1:1–2). Many charismatic brothers agree that nothing they receive may add to Scripture or overrule it, and this commentary gladly recognises that common ground while holding that the revelatory gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation.

What it does not mean. Inerrancy does not mean every passage is to be read literally regardless of its genre; poetry, parable and prophecy are to be read as what they are. And sufficiency does not mean Scripture tells us everything about everything (like science or medicine), but everything we need for salvation and godliness (2 Peter 1:3).

What about the apparent contradictions and errors people point to? Take them seriously, and take them humbly. Many dissolve on careful reading: different writers report different details of the same event, round numbers, arrange material by theme rather than date, or speak in ordinary language about the sky and the sunrise, as we still do. Others are explained by the history of copying, and responsible Bibles note such places openly; the original text is preserved with remarkable care, and no doctrine depends on a doubtful reading. A few remain hard, and it is honest to say so. But the God who breathed out Scripture does not lie, and over two centuries of scrutiny many confident claims of error have been answered by archaeology and better understanding. When you meet a difficulty, keep reading, ask for help, and give God the benefit of the doubt you would give a trusted friend.

Is it not circular to trust the Bible because it says it is from God? Every final authority is in that position: if something higher could certify it, that higher thing would be the final authority instead. Even reason cannot prove itself without using reason. But the claim does not hang in the air. It comes with a risen Lord who treated these writings as his Father’s word (John 10:35), with promises made centuries ahead and kept in him, with one message running through some forty writers and fifteen centuries, and with lives changed by it. Above all, the Spirit who breathed it out opens blind eyes to see its glory, so that a believer trusts it as he trusts the sun, by its own light (1 Corinthians 2:12–14). Read it, and let it speak for itself.

How do I read the Bible so that it does all four things in me? Read it regularly, and read all of it over time, not only favourite passages. Come expecting God to speak, and ask four questions of each passage: what does this teach me about God and his ways? Where does it show me I am wrong? How does it set me right, especially through Christ? What habit of righteousness does it train me in? Read with others, under good preaching, so that you are not only reading your own opinions back into it. And then obey what you have seen, because training in righteousness happens in practice, not in the armchair. The Bible is not a book you master; it is a book through which God masters you.

Does the sufficiency of Scripture mean I should not see a doctor or a counsellor? No. Scripture is sufficient for what it was given for: to make us wise for salvation and to equip us for godliness. It does not claim to replace medicine, any more than it replaces plumbing; Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. Medical and psychological help can be a gift of God’s common grace. What sufficiency means is that no other source has authority to overrule Scripture about who you are, what is right and wrong, and how to be reconciled to God. Use every good help, and test every help by the word.

On a Tuesday. The Bible on the kitchen table is the voice of God, as truly as the voice at Sinai, only gentler. A short prayer before reading, Lord, correct me today, turns a habit into a meeting. And the part of the Bible you have quietly shelved, Leviticus perhaps, or a minor prophet, is God-breathed too, and Christ is waiting there.

For worship. God is not silent. The same breath that spoke the stars into being has breathed out a book, and in it he speaks to us as a father to his children: teaching, rebuking, lifting us up, training us for the long years. He did not leave us to grope for him in the dark. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away.
