4.title: Preach the Word: The Commission, the Crown, and the Cloak
4.overview:
Paul’s last chapter has two halves. First the charge, sworn before the Judge of the living and the dead: preach the word, in season and out, because people will gather teachers who tell them what they want to hear. Keep your head, endure, evangelise, finish your ministry. Then Paul’s own finish: he is being poured out like a drink offering, he has fought the good fight and kept the faith, and a crown is waiting, for him and for all who love Christ’s appearing.

The second half is among the most human passages Paul wrote: friends gone and one friend staying, a failed man restored, a cloak and books sent for, a hearing where everyone left but the Lord stood by him. The last word Paul wrote is “grace”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Preach the Word, and Finish the Race
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final charge, given with Christ’s judgement in view, and the reason it is urgent: a time when people lose their appetite for the truth. Then Paul’s own finish, a life poured out and a crown waiting, not only for him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Last Charge, and the Steward's Report

Paul swears Timothy before the court that will judge both him and Nero (v. 1), and his ‘I have kept the faith’ (v. 7) is a steward's report, not a boast. The crown is for all who have loved Christ's appearing (v. 8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The itch is in the hearers' ears (v. 3): they assemble teachers to suit themselves.

Now: When did one of your teachers last tell you something you did not want to hear?

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Timothy 4 contains Paul’s last recorded words. Before God and Christ the coming Judge, Timothy must preach the word in season and out of season, because people will soon collect teachers who tell them what they want to hear (vv. 1–4); he must keep his head, endure hardship, evangelise and complete his ministry (v. 5). Paul is already being poured out like a drink offering; he has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith, and the crown of righteousness awaits him and all who love Christ’s appearing (vv. 6–8). Then the personal close (vv. 9–22): Demas has deserted him and only Luke remains; bring Mark, the cloak and the parchments; beware of Alexander. Everyone deserted him at his first hearing, but the Lord stood by him and will bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom. Greetings, a plea to come before winter, and grace. It is not a farewell to hope but a man walking toward a crown, with the Lord beside him.

I charge you in the presence of God. Few charges in Paul’s letters are more solemn. The verb is solemnly testify, adjure, as in 2:14 and 1 Timothy 5:21: a court-like oath. Paul is about to be judged by a Roman court. He swears Timothy by a different one. And the presence of God is not a figure of speech. It is the presence of the one from whose sight no creature is hidden, whose eyes are like a flame of fire (Hebrews 4:13; Revelation 1:14). Timothy will open the Scriptures under that gaze, and every hearer will sit under it too.

Who is to judge the living and the dead. Christ will judge everyone, those alive at his return and those who have died (Acts 10:42; 17:31; John 5:22). This court will have both Paul and Nero in front of it. Ministers will give account (Hebrews 13:17; James 3:1). The phrase passed into the Apostles’ Creed, and the church has confessed it ever since: from thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.

And by his appearing and his kingdom. “Appearing” (epiphaneia) is his visible return (1 Timothy 6:14), the shining-out of the King, and the kingdom is his rule fully revealed. Everything Timothy does in Ephesus is to be done with that day in view.

Preach the word. Then the charge itself, in short imperatives that come like hammer blows: five here, and four more in verse 5. “Preach” is the herald’s verb, to announce publicly what someone else has given you to say. A herald does not compose his message or improve it; he delivers it. And the object is definite: the word, the message of God, the Scriptures just described (3:15–17). Not the preacher’s opinions, philosophy or personal stories, but God’s word.

Be ready in season and out of season. Stand by, be on hand. The phrase is literally well-timed, ill-timed: when it is welcome and when it is not. It concedes that there will be plenty of the second kind, and tells him to be standing by anyway, whether people want to hear or not, whether he feels like it or not. Unpopularity must not silence the word; this is not a licence for tactlessness in personal conversation.

Reprove, rebuke, and exhort. Three verbs covering the range of what preaching does. “Reprove” is to convict, to show a man he is wrong, correcting the mind, as in 3:16. “Rebuke” is the sharper word, a warning that addresses the will. “Exhort” is to call alongside, encourage, appeal, comfort the heart. Two hard and one warm, and a ministry with only the first two is a bludgeon while one with only the third is a comfortable fraud.

With complete patience and teaching. And then the two qualifiers that govern all of it. Patience, because people change slowly, and the word is the long-tempered one, slow to take offence. Teaching, because reproof without instruction leaves a man knowing he is wrong and not knowing what is right. Rebuke without patience becomes harshness; exhortation without teaching becomes empty.

The patience of the Judge. The charge holds together two things that seem to pull apart: the Judge is coming, and the preacher must be patient. They belong together because the Judge himself is patient now. Paul knew it from the inside. Christ Jesus showed him, the foremost of sinners, his perfect patience, as an example to everyone who would believe (1 Timothy 1:16), and the same word, makrothymia, stands here. The Lord delays the day of judgement not from slowness but because he is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). So the herald’s long-suffering is not softness about judgement. It is Christ’s own patience carried in his messenger’s voice, while the door is still open.

What is the difference between preaching the word and giving a good talk? A good talk may be interesting, helpful and even true, and still not be preaching the word. Preaching the word means the message comes out of the text of Scripture and is governed by it: the preacher explains what the passage says, shows how it points to Christ, and presses it on the hearers as God’s own message to them. The authority is in the word, not in the speaker’s personality, stories or opinions. Illustrations, warmth and clarity are good servants. The test is simple: after the sermon, do you know better what God has said, and do you see Christ more clearly?

I sit in the pew, not the pulpit. What does this charge mean for me? It tells you what to look for and what to pray for. Look for a church where the word is preached faithfully, including the reproof and rebuke, and not only the comfort. Pray for your pastor, that he will be ready in season and out of season and will not soften the message to please. Listen as one who will also give account: come prepared, open your Bible, receive correction without resentment, and act on what you hear. And in your own conversations, be ready to speak a word from Scripture when it is needed, gently and patiently.

For worship. The Judge of the living and the dead is the same Jesus who was judged in our place. Pilate sat on the bench and the Son of God stood in the dock; one day the positions will be reversed for ever, and every knee will bow. Until then he speaks, through the plain preaching of his word, and his word does not return to him empty.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People will not endure sound teaching. Paul now gives the reason the charge is so heavy, and it is not that people will attack the truth but that they will lose their appetite for it. “Endure” is to put up with, to tolerate. And “sound” is the medical word again: wholesome, healthy, the diet that keeps a body well. Sound teaching confronts sin and pride, and people will refuse to tolerate it. That is a reason to preach urgently now (v. 2).

But having itching ears. Literally having the hearing tickled: ears that want to be scratched with something pleasant, new, flattering, entertaining. And note where the itch is: in the hearers, not the teachers. Paul locates the demand side first, which is uncomfortable, because we generally blame bad teachers for bad churches. He says the market comes before the supply. Underneath the itch is a heart that wants God’s blessing without God’s rule, and wants teachers who will recruit God to serve its comfort and success. Anyone can now assemble a set of teachers who agree with him, more easily than at any point in history, and can do it while believing he is being discerning.

They will accumulate teachers. The verb means to heap up: a pile of teachers, which suggests both quantity and choice. The criterion is stated without embarrassment: according to their own desires. They will select for agreement. And “for themselves” is doing quiet work. These are not people misled by a teacher who arrived; they went out and assembled a collection.

And wander off into myths. The two movements of verse 4 are one motion: a deliberate turning away, and then being turned aside, as in 1 Timothy 1:6. A person who stops listening to the truth does not become neutral; there is always something to drift into. When people reject truth, they do not believe nothing; they believe fables (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).

The teacher the crowds left. Jesus himself knew what it was for people to stop enduring sound words. When he told the crowd that he was the bread of life and that they must feed on him, many of his disciples said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?” and many turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:60, 66). They had wanted a Messiah who would fill their stomachs and leave their hearts alone (John 6:26). The answer to this verse is Peter’s answer that day: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). The truth people turn from is finally not a system but a person, who said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a popular preacher must be unfaithful, or an unpopular one faithful. Popularity is not the test; faithfulness to the word is.

Is it wrong to listen to preachers online, beyond my own church? Not in itself. Good preaching online and in books has fed many believers, especially the housebound and those in places with no faithful church. The danger is the one Paul names: heaping up teachers for yourself, sampling until you find voices that confirm what you already want. Online listening should supplement, never replace, belonging to a local church, where you are known, shepherded and corrected by elders who watch for your soul (Hebrews 13:17). Choose a few sound teachers rather than many, and notice whether any of them ever unsettle you. If none does, the selection may be yours and not God’s.

What if the preaching in my church is weak, though faithful? Be patient, and be a help. Faithful but plain preaching, which explains Scripture accurately and points to Christ, is far better than gifted preaching that drifts from the word. Pray for your pastor, encourage him specifically when he helps you, and come hungry; much depends on the ears as well as the mouth. If the preaching has actually departed from the gospel, that is a different matter: Paul tells believers to keep themselves clear of what is dishonourable (2:20–21), and it may then be right to look for a faithful church. But do not leave a faithful church for a more entertaining one; that is precisely the itch this verse describes.

For worship. God loves us too much to scratch our ears. He tells us the truth about our sin, because only the truth can lead us to the Saviour, and he tells us the truth about his Son, which is better than every fable ever invented. The myths of men promise much and deliver nothing. The gospel promises everything and has delivered it in a crucified and risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, always be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for you, always be sober-minded. “As for you” is the contrast that has run through these letters, the third time in two chapters (3:10, 14), and four final imperatives follow. “Be sober-minded” is clear-headed, alert, literally free from intoxication. In a church where people are accumulating teachers to scratch their ears, Timothy is to keep his head: not swept away by enthusiasms or intoxicated by fables, but steady and watchful (1 Thessalonians 5:6, 8; 1 Peter 5:8). It is not a glamorous instruction, and it is the first one.

Endure suffering. The same root as the sharing in suffering of 1:8 and 2:3. And Paul has already named the resource: God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power, and the suffering is shared by the power of God (1:7–8).

Do the work of an evangelist. An evangelist is a bringer of good news, and the word occurs only three times in the New Testament (here; Acts 21:8; Ephesians 4:11). Timothy’s job in Ephesus was largely corrective, assessing elders, silencing false teachers, managing a widows’ roll, and it would be easy for such a man to spend his whole ministry on maintenance. Paul tells him to keep announcing the good news to people who have not heard it. And it is called a work: a task to be done rather than only a gift some possess. Pastoral work and evangelism belong together.

The good news has a name. The hardship and the evangelism are tied together by the gospel Paul has already set before Timothy: remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering (2:8–9). The good news an evangelist brings is not an idea but a person, the Son of David who died and rose. And the suffering Timothy must endure has the shape of that gospel, the road of a Lord who went through the cross to the crown; so the letter can promise that if we endure, we will also reign with him (2:12). Timothy is not asked to suffer for a cause. He is asked to share the road of the one he announces.

Fulfill your ministry. Carry it out completely, leave nothing undone: much the same charge Paul sent to Archippus (Colossians 4:17). Paul has finished his course (v. 7); Timothy must finish his. And it is your ministry, not Paul’s: Timothy is not asked to be a second Paul. A dying apostle’s final instruction is not a grand vision but a short list any Christian could be handed.

Is evangelist an office today, and must every Christian evangelise? Christ gives evangelists to the church (Ephesians 4:11), like Philip (Acts 21:8), and the church still sends people to preach the gospel where it is not known. Timothy, as a pastor, was to do the evangelist’s work. Every believer is to be ready to speak of Christ (1 Peter 3:15), though not all are gifted as evangelists.

What is my ministry, if I am not a pastor? It is the particular service God has given you in the place he has put you. Every believer has a ministry in this sense: the gifts you have been given (1 Peter 4:10), the people God has placed around you, your family, your church, your neighbours and colleagues, and the opportunities that open in front of you. A mother raising children in the Lord, an elderly widow who prays, a teenager inviting a friend to church, a deacon who visits the sick: each has a ministry to fulfil. Do not compare yours with someone else’s. Ask what the Lord has given you to do, and do it to the end.

On a Tuesday. Pray for an opportunity to share the gospel with one person you know this week, and be ready with a short, clear account of what Christ has done.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already being poured out. Here is the reason for the four commands: Timothy must fulfil his ministry because Paul has finished his. “Poured out as a drink offering” is one word, spendomai. In the Old Testament a drink offering of wine was poured out with a sacrifice, accompanying and completing it (Numbers 15:1–10; 28:7): a small offering, given at the altar alongside the greater one. From an earlier prison Paul used the image as a possibility: even if I am to be poured out (Philippians 2:17). Here the condition is gone, and the word “already” says the pouring has started.

And the time of my departure has come. “Departure” is analysis, the noun matching the verb of Philippians 1:23, where Paul wrote of his desire to depart and be with Christ. It means a loosing, a release, and its related verb was used of untying a ship from the quay, striking a tent, freeing a prisoner from his chains. Each pictures a release into something beyond, and Paul chooses it for what is about to happen to him at Roman hands. He is not speculating about the future. The thing is here.

Priest, not victim. The image also reclassifies what is being done to him. Rome believes it is disposing of a troublesome provincial. Paul describes an altar. And the composure of the sentence is remarkable: there is no panic in it and no resignation either. A man probably weeks or months from execution reaches for the language of the altar and of a boat casting off, and in the next breath asks Timothy to bring his coat.

The sacrifice behind the drink offering. A drink offering was never the sacrifice itself; it was poured beside one. Paul does not name the sacrifice here (in Philippians 2:17 it was the offering of his converts’ faith), but every Christian offering rests on one that came first. Isaiah said the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and Jesus said of the cup that it was his blood of the covenant, poured out for many (Mark 14:24). Christ was poured out completely, and his offering needed nothing added. Paul’s death is the small libation of a grateful servant, the last act of a life offered as a living sacrifice in view of God’s mercies (Romans 12:1). A Christian’s death can be worship because Christ’s death was atonement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s death atones for sin. Christ’s sacrifice alone does that (Hebrews 10:14). Paul’s death is an offering of thanksgiving and devotion.

What happens to a believer at the moment of death? The soul goes immediately and consciously into the presence of Christ, while the body rests in the grave until the resurrection. Jesus told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and Paul says to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory: the souls of believers are made perfect in holiness and pass into glory (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). That is why Paul uses a word for setting sail. At the resurrection, when Christ returns, the body is raised and reunited with the soul, glorified, and the whole person enters the new creation.

How can a Christian face death without fear? Not by pretending it is nothing; death is an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and it is natural to feel its weight. But Christ has drawn its sting by bearing our sin, and death can no longer condemn us (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). For the believer, death is a departure to be with Christ, which is far better. Many believers who feared death for years have found grace when the hour came; God gives strength for the day, not before it. Prepare by living close to Christ now, by setting your affairs in order, by speaking to your family about your hope, and by meditating on what is waiting. It is not wrong to want to live longer for the sake of others (Philippians 1:24). It is a gift to be able to go in peace.

On a Tuesday. Think about your own departure, not morbidly but honestly. If you knew it were near, what would you want to say to the people you love? Say one of those things this week.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering of wine was poured out over a sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have fought the good fight. Three clauses, all in the Greek perfect, which describes something completed whose result stands: not I fought and it is over, but I have fought, and it is done. The image is the contest of the arena, or perhaps the battlefield. It is the charge he gave Timothy in the first letter (1 Timothy 6:12), now reported of himself in the past tense. And the fight was good, noble. He does not say he won every engagement. He says the contest was worth entering, and he has stayed in it to the end.

I have finished the race. The word for race is a course with a marked end. Paul had used it years earlier at Miletus, telling the Ephesian elders he only wanted to finish his course and the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus (Acts 20:24). He wanted one thing, for years, and here at the end he can say he got it.

I have kept the faith. The verb is the guarding word: held fast, preserved, the same idea as the deposit of 1:14. And the phrase can be read two ways, both true. He has kept faith, remained faithful to Christ, as one keeps a promise; and he has kept the faith, the body of truth entrusted to him, guarding the deposit unchanged (1:14; 1 Timothy 6:20). Given how this letter has hammered the deposit, the second is surely primary.

The keeper behind the keeping. Every clause of this verse points past Paul to his Lord. The race was the course he received from the Lord Jesus (Acts 20:24); the faith he kept is the gospel of Christ, the deposit of 1:14; and he could keep it because he was kept. At the start of this letter he wrote, I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me (1:12). Paul guarded the gospel, and Christ was guarding it, and him, all along. That is what grace looks like at the finish line: the man who says I have kept is a man who has been held, through floggings, shipwreck and prison, by a Saviour from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28).

A steward’s report. Paul has written in this letter that grace was given before the ages began and not because of works (1:9), in the first letter he called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15), and in this chapter he says the Lord strengthened him (v. 17), so this cannot be self-congratulation. It is a steward’s report, not a claim. And it is a rare thing that anyone can say it. Most people arrive at the end with things unfinished and are not sure what they were for. Paul knew what he had been given to do, did it, and could say so without either false modesty or pride. That is the fruit of a life with one aim in it (3:10).

I have failed so often. Could I ever say these words? Yes, if you mean by them what Paul meant. He was not claiming a flawless record; he had been a persecutor, and he wrote openly of his struggles with sin (Romans 7:15–25). He meant that by grace he had not given up: he stayed in the contest, kept running, and did not let go of Christ or the gospel. Every believer who perseveres to the end in faith can say the same, and every true believer will, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The fight includes many falls and many restorations. What matters is that you are still in it when the bell rings, and that is his gift.

What does keeping the faith look like for an ordinary Christian? It means holding on to the gospel you received and not exchanging it for something more fashionable: believing what Scripture teaches about Christ, sin and salvation when it is unpopular, and teaching it unchanged to those who come after you. And it means keeping faith with Christ in your life: staying loyal to him through suffering, temptation and long dull years; going on praying, gathering with his people, confessing sin, and trusting his promises. Most of it happens in ordinary weeks, not dramatic moments. A grandmother who believed and taught the Scriptures for sixty years has kept the faith as truly as an apostle.

On a Tuesday. Most of the race is run on ordinary days: getting up to pray when tired, going to church when it is raining, saying no to the same temptation again. None of it feels like a good fight, but that is what the fight mostly is, and the Lord who kept Paul is holding you through it by his Spirit.

For worship. There was one who fought the fight, finished the race and kept the faith perfectly, and he did it for us. Jesus is the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). He ran without one stumble, did always the things that please his Father (John 8:29), and lost none of those given to him. Our running is never flawless, but his perfect race is counted to everyone who trusts him, and he stands at the end of ours holding the crown.

verseByVerse.quote: Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Henceforth there is laid up for me. From now on, what remains: the settled state of affairs from this point. And “laid up” means reserved, stored, put by for someone. It is already there, waiting, with his name on it, kept safe in heaven (Colossians 1:5; 1 Peter 1:4).

The crown of righteousness. The crown is the victor’s wreath at the games (2:5) rather than a royal diadem: the athletic image running to its end. The prize is being finally and fully right with God, which is what Paul spent his life insisting could not be earned. The phrase “of righteousness” has been read three ways (a crown that is righteousness, a crown rewarding a righteous life, a crown given by the righteous Judge), and the first fits best, given by the righteous Judge of the next clause. Vindication means being declared in the right in public, as Christ himself was vindicated when God raised him from the dead (1 Timothy 3:16). This is the public completion of justification. In justification God pronounces the believing sinner righteous, his own record set aside and Christ’s obedience and death reckoned to his account (Romans 4:5; 5:1). That verdict is given the moment a person believes; on that day it will be announced before the whole creation. Other crowns in the New Testament, of life (James 1:12; Revelation 2:10), of glory (1 Peter 5:4), imperishable (1 Corinthians 9:25), are different ways of describing the one reward of eternal life with Christ.

Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award. Paul is awaiting the verdict of a Roman court which he expects to find against him. He looks past it to a different bench, and calls that judge righteous, which is precisely what the one in Rome is not. Christ will reverse the earthly verdict on that day, the day of his return (1:12, 18). There is real comfort here for anyone who has been treated unjustly and can do nothing about it. Paul does not deny the injustice or minimise it. He appeals it to a higher court, and waits.

But also to all who have loved his appearing. Then the clause that opens the whole thing outward, and it is the reason this verse belongs to every Christian. The crown is not a special award for apostles or martyrs. The qualification is simple: those who have longed for Christ to come. Not those who finished a race comparable to Paul’s, but those who loved the thought of seeing him. The tense is perfect again: have loved, and go on loving. It is a settled affection, and a fair test of where a person’s treasure is. A man tells you what he loves by what he hopes is coming.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul earned salvation by his works. The crown is a gracious reward. As Augustine said, when God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts.

I do not long for Christ’s return. Sometimes I dread it. What does that mean? Ask why. If you dread it because you love this world more than him, that is a warning to heed (Demas deserted Paul because he was in love with this present world, v. 10), and the remedy is to go to Christ and ask him to change your loves. But many believers dread it for other reasons: fear of judgement, confusion about what will happen, or simply because life is good and they cannot imagine anything better. Then let Scripture fill your imagination. For those in Christ, his appearing means no condemnation, the end of sin and grief, the resurrection of the body, reunion with believing loved ones, and seeing the face of the one who loved you. The more you know him, the more you will want him to come.

Is it wrong to be motivated by reward? No, if the reward is rightly understood. Jesus himself motivates his disciples with reward (Matthew 6:19–21; 5:12), and Moses looked to the reward (Hebrews 11:26). The reward is not wages earned but a gift of grace, and at its heart it is Christ himself: to be right with God for ever and to be with him. Wanting that is not mercenary; it is what love wants. What would be wrong is serving in order to put God in our debt. Scripture also suggests that faithful service will be acknowledged on that day (1 Corinthians 3:12–14), yet every crown will be cast before the throne, because every crown was his gift.

On a Tuesday. This week, end your prayers with the last prayer of the Bible: Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20). Notice what in your life makes it hard to pray that honestly, and bring that to him too.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The personal close of Paul’s last letter: a lonely man in a cell, the friends who left and those who stayed, an injury handed over to the Lord, and the Lord who stood by him when no one else did and will bring him safely home.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kinds of Wrong, Two Different Prayers

Of Alexander Paul says only that the Lord will repay (v. 14); of the friends who deserted him he prays ‘may it not be charged against them’ (v. 16). It is Stephen's prayer (Acts 7:60), prayed thirty years on by the man who once held the coats.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Demas left for love of this present world; Mark, once refused, is sent for as ‘very useful’ (vv. 10–11).

Now: Five verses after the crown of righteousness, Paul asks for his cloak and his books (v. 13): faith that does not pretend the body's needs are beneath notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to come to me soon. For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry. Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do your best to come to me soon. After the crown and the righteous judge, this. The apostle who has just written of the crown laid up for him asks a young man to hurry up and visit (the verb of 2:15). He is lonely, and his time is short.

For Demas has deserted me. Then the reason, and it is a roll-call of absence. We met Demas twice before, sending greetings alongside Luke in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24: a fellow worker, one of the circle. And the charge is not heresy or scandal. He loved this present age. The contrast with verse 8 is deliberate: some love Christ’s appearing; Demas loved the present age. “Deserted” is forsaken, left in the lurch. Perhaps he was afraid, perhaps drawn by comfort or opportunity; he went to Thessalonica, possibly his home town. That is how most people leave: not with a repudiation but with a preference. Something ordinary and legitimate, comfort, safety, a quieter life, became more attractive than a chained old man in Rome. Nobody would have accused Demas of anything at the time.

The age Christ died to rescue us from. This present world is literally the now age, and Paul had told the Galatians what Christ did about it: he gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age (Galatians 1:4). Demas fell in love with the very order of things from which his Lord had died to set him free. That is why the two loves of verses 8 and 10 cannot share one heart. To love Christ’s appearing is to long for the age he will bring; to love the now age is, in the end, to prefer that he stay away.

Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Crescens is otherwise unknown. Galatia could be the region in central Turkey, or possibly Gaul (France), as some manuscripts read. Titus had moved on from Crete (Titus 1:5; 3:12) to Dalmatia, on the Adriatic coast. No blame attaches to these two; they have gone on ministry, not deserted. But the room is empty either way.

Luke alone is with me. The beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), author of the Gospel and Acts, the man who travelled with Paul through the shipwreck and wrote the account of it, is still there in a Roman cell when everyone else has gone.

Get Mark and bring him. The sentence is lovely for what it does not say. He is the John Mark who abandoned Paul and Barnabas mid-journey (Acts 13:13) and caused so sharp a disagreement with Barnabas that the two men parted (Acts 15:37–40). Paul had refused to take him. Here, at the end of everything, he sends for him, and the word he uses is useful, the word Paul used of Onesimus, whose very name means useful, when he asked Philemon to see it in another failed man (Philemon 11). There is no defensiveness in it and no revisiting of the old argument. A man who once wrote a colleague off asks for him by name in his final letter, and the church has received from Mark, as early tradition holds, the Gospel that bears his name. Grace restores the failed, and it also restores the people who gave up on them.

Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus. Tychicus was a trusted messenger who carried Paul’s letters to Ephesus and Colossae (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7). Perhaps he carried this letter, and would replace Timothy in Ephesus while Timothy came to Rome. Even alone in a cell, Paul is still arranging for the churches to be cared for.

Did Demas lose his salvation, or was he never saved? Scripture does not tell us his end. If he never returned, the Reformed reading is that he showed he had never truly belonged (1 John 2:19); Arminian Christians (who hold that a true believer can finally fall away) would read him as a believer who did. He may have repented. His story is a warning to love Christ’s appearing (v. 8) more than this present world.

What does loving this present world look like now? It rarely looks like wild sin. It looks like Demas: a quiet preference for comfort, safety and success over Christ and his people. It is choosing the promotion that takes you away from any faithful church without a second thought; drifting from fellowship because Sundays are full; avoiding a suffering friend because it is depressing; deciding that following Christ wholeheartedly can wait until life is less busy. The world here is not creation or people, whom God loves, but the present age organised without God (1 John 2:15–17). The test is what you would give up for Christ, and what you are giving up Christ for.

Someone failed me badly, or I failed someone. Can it really be restored? Mark is God’s answer that it can. Restoration needs repentance from the one who failed, which Mark evidently showed over years of faithful service, and a readiness in the one who was wronged to see the grace of God at work and to say so. It does not mean pretending the failure did not happen, or rushing trust before it is earned. But it does mean refusing to define a brother for ever by his worst moment. If you were the one who failed, keep serving faithfully; God can make you useful again. If you were the one wronged, look for the signs of change, and be willing to send for Mark.

On a Tuesday. Every church has someone in Paul’s position, lonely in the faith: the elderly, the imprisoned, the missionary far from home. A Luke is simply a person who stays.

For worship. The Lord who restored Mark is the Lord who restored Peter, and who has restored every one of us. He makes the unprofitable profitable, and turns deserters into Gospel writers. And he never deserts: when Demas leaves and the room empties, he remains, the friend who sticks closer than a brother.
verseByVerse.note: Mark, who had once deserted Paul, is now “very useful.” Dalmatia lay on the Adriatic coast.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bring the cloak. It is a deeply human verse, and it comes five verses after the crown of righteousness. The same man, in the same paragraph, thinks about eternity and about being cold. The cloak was a heavy outer garment, a circular woollen cape with a hole for the head, the kind a poor man might own only one of. Carpus is otherwise unknown. Troas was a port in northwest Turkey, on Timothy’s route to Rome; Paul may have been arrested there suddenly and left his things. A Roman prison in winter is a serious matter for a man no longer young, which is why he asks Timothy to come before winter (v. 21).

Also the books, and above all the parchments. The books are scrolls, probably papyrus rolls. Parchments were made from animal skin, more durable and far more expensive than papyrus. Most likely they were portions of the Old Testament Scriptures; possibly notebooks, copies of Paul’s own letters, or legal documents such as proof of his Roman citizenship. Whatever they were, he wanted them enough to say above all. A man who has written that he has finished the race, weeks or months from execution, sends across the empire for something to read. He is not winding down: a mind still learning to the end.

Tyndale’s echo. William Tyndale, imprisoned at Vilvoorde in the winter before he was strangled and burned, wrote to the governor asking for a warmer cap, a woollen shirt, and above all his Hebrew Bible, grammar and dictionary. Whether or not he intended the echo of this verse, it shows how exactly one prisoner understood another.

A Lord who knew the cold. Paul’s request is not beneath the gospel, because the gospel is about a Son who took a real body. The Word became flesh (John 1:14): he grew tired at a well (John 4:6), had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and on the cross said, I thirst (John 19:28). We have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and that includes a body shivering in a cell. Faith of the sort this letter describes does not float above the body’s needs; it asks for a coat. And that Lord will raise the cold, worn body of his servant in glory.

Is it unspiritual to ask for practical help? Not at all. Paul, an apostle, asks plainly for a coat, and earlier thanked Onesiphorus for practical refreshment (1:16) and the Philippians for money (Philippians 4:14–18). Pride sometimes dresses itself as spirituality and refuses to admit need. Humility asks. God usually meets our needs through his people, and letting them help you is part of how the body of Christ works (Galatians 6:2). Pray, certainly, and trust him; and then tell a brother or sister what you need.

Should Christians read widely, or only the Bible? Paul wanted his books as well as the parchments, and above all the parchments. That is the right order. Scripture comes first and governs everything else, but other good reading, theology, history, biography, literature, can feed the mind and serve faith; Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28). Read with discernment, testing all things by the word. And keep learning as long as you live. A believer who stops reading at forty often stops growing too.

On a Tuesday. Somewhere this winter a believer is cold, or short of something to read, or waiting for a letter that does not come. A coat, a book or a few lines in an envelope are not small things to the person receiving them; Paul thought them worth a sentence of Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: With winter coming (v. 21), Paul wants his heavy cloak; the parchments may have been copies of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. Beware of him yourself, for he strongly opposed our message.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alexander the coppersmith. A metalworker, possibly the Alexander of 1 Timothy 1:20, whom Paul had handed over to Satan, or possibly the Alexander of the Ephesian riot (Acts 19:33), though the name was very common. We are not told what he did. The word for harm is strong: he showed me much evil. Perhaps he informed against Paul, testified against him, or caused his arrest, which would make him the reason Paul is in this cell.

The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. The Lord repays both the faithful and the wicked (Psalm 62:12). Some manuscripts and older translations read a wish, may the Lord repay him, but the better reading is a plain future: will repay. Paul is not cursing. He is stating what will happen, and leaving it there. He has been badly injured and does not pretend otherwise, or produce a strained forgiveness that denies the damage. But he does not retaliate, and he does not ask God to retaliate on his behalf. He hands the account over, exactly as he taught: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19). Committing judgement to God is what forgiveness does. A Christian can let an injury go not because it did not matter but because it will be dealt with by someone better placed to do it.

Beware of him yourself. He was apparently near Timothy, or Timothy would pass through his area on the way to Rome, and Paul tells him there is a dangerous man in the way. His vehement opposition was to the gospel, not merely to Paul personally. The warning is practical rather than bitter. Forgiveness never required anybody to be naive, and warning a young colleague about a person who has proved dangerous is not gossip but protection.

The same hands crown and repay. The Lord who will repay Alexander is the Lord of verse 8, the righteous judge who will award the crown: the verb is the same, and so are the hands. That is why Paul can let go. He is not handing the injury to an indifferent fate but to Christ, who knows exactly what was done to his servant and to his gospel. And Paul learned the letting go from Christ himself, who, when he was reviled, did not revile in return, but kept entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). The one who will judge Alexander first showed Paul how to wait for judgement without bitterness.

Is it wrong to want justice for what someone did to me? No. Wanting wrong to be put right is part of being made in the image of a just God, and the psalms are full of cries for justice. What is forbidden is taking vengeance yourself, or nursing hatred. Paul shows the way: name the harm truthfully, refuse personal revenge, hand the case to the Lord, and keep praying, even for your enemy’s repentance (Matthew 5:44). God has also given human authorities to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), so seeking lawful justice, reporting a crime or abuse, is not unforgiving. You can forgive from the heart and still let the courts do their work.

How do I forgive someone and still warn others about them? By keeping two duties distinct. Forgiveness means releasing your claim to pay them back and wishing them good, including repentance and salvation. Protection means telling the truth where others are at risk. Paul did both in two verses. So if a person has abused, defrauded or deceived, you may and sometimes must warn those who could be harmed, report it to the proper authorities, and keep appropriate distance. Abuse is never to be covered up in the name of forgiveness. What you avoid is spreading the story further than protection requires, or speaking with relish. Warn as Paul did: briefly, factually, for the sake of others.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth will do right. Not one injury done to his people will be overlooked, and not one will be punished twice: either it was borne by Christ at the cross for those who repent, or it will be answered in full on the last day. And the mercy of that cross is wider than our wounds. The man who wrote this verse once did great harm to the church himself, breathing threats against the Lord’s disciples, and the Lord he persecuted made him an apostle (Acts 9:1, 15; 1 Timothy 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them! But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion's mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one came to stand by me. The phrase is a legal one. The “first defence” was a preliminary hearing of his case under Roman law, before the main trial, where a defendant would ordinarily have friends come alongside him, speak for his character, or serve as advocates. Paul had none. Every one of them stayed away, and “deserted” is the same word as with Demas (v. 10).

May it not be charged against them! It is the only response he makes. And it is Stephen’s prayer as the stones came in: Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:60), which Paul heard, standing there approving, while the coats were laid at his feet (Acts 7:58; 8:1). Some thirty years later, deserted himself, he prays the prayer he once watched a dying man pray, and the prayer his Lord prayed on the cross (Luke 23:34; a verse missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, though widely held to be genuine). He does not excuse them. It was a sin; that is why it might be charged. He simply asks that it not be. They were weak and afraid, not malicious, unlike Alexander.

But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me. The words answer each other: no one came to stand by him, and then the Lord did. It is the whole comfort of the passage. The support Paul was owed and did not get was supplied by someone else, in the same room, at the same hour (Acts 23:11; Hebrews 13:5). “Strengthened” is the same word as 1 Timothy 1:12 and 2 Timothy 2:1.

That all the Gentiles might hear it. And the purpose is characteristic: not that Paul might be acquitted, but that the message might be fully proclaimed. He was strengthened in order to preach, at his own capital trial, to whoever was in the room. He had spent his life as the apostle to the Gentiles (Acts 9:15), and his defence became a sermon heard in the capital of the Gentile world.

So I was rescued from the lion’s mouth. A proverbial expression for deadly danger, drawn from the Psalms and Daniel (Psalm 22:21; Daniel 6:20–22). Some think of literal lions in the arena, or of Nero, or Satan (1 Peter 5:8), but it probably means simply mortal danger. Whatever the immediate reference, the hearing did not end in sentence: he lived to write this letter.

In the flow. These verses gather up the whole letter. The desertion of Asia (1:15) is repeated in a Roman courtroom. The Lord who strengthens Paul is the source of the strength Timothy was told to draw on (2:1). The message fully proclaimed at the hearing shows the word still unbound while the apostle is chained (2:9). And Paul’s confidence that the Lord will bring him safely into his kingdom is the confidence of 1:12, now spoken at the edge of death. The letter has asked Timothy not to be ashamed and to share in suffering; here Paul shows him what that looks like, and who stands beside the man who does it.

From every evil deed. The word echoes the Lord’s Prayer: deliver us from evil (Matthew 6:13). But not from death; Paul knows he will die (v. 6). From every evil attack that would destroy his faith or his soul. The rescue he expects is through the execution and into the kingdom. That is what Christian confidence actually looks like at close range: not the assurance that nothing bad will happen, but that nothing bad can finally prevent the arrival. And so comes his last doxology. Facing death, deserted by his friends, cold and waiting for execution, Paul ends in praise: to him be the glory for ever and ever.

I have felt abandoned, and I did not feel the Lord standing by me. What then? Many believers have known that darkness, and Scripture does not hide it (Psalm 88; Psalm 22:1). Feelings are not the measure of his presence. His promise is: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), and he kept it even when you could not sense it, which is why you are still holding on. Look back and you may see strength you were given without noticing it. Tell him honestly how it feels, as the psalmists did. Read the Gospels and watch how he treats the lonely. And go to his people, because one of the ways he stands by us is by sending an Onesiphorus, who searched Rome for Paul until he found him (1:16–17), or a Luke, who stayed when the others had gone (v. 11).

How do I pray for people who failed me when I needed them? Pray the way Paul did: may it not be charged against them. That is not saying it did not matter; it is asking God to forgive them as he has forgiven you. Name the failure honestly to God, admit the hurt, and then deliberately ask for their good. You may need to pray it many times before your heart agrees with your words; that is normal. It may also be right, in time, to speak to them, gently. But the first step is to release them into God’s mercy, which is where you yourself have been standing all along.

On a Tuesday. If you are facing something alone this week, a hearing, a diagnosis, a hard conversation, ask the Lord beforehand to stand by you, and ask also that through it his name may be made known. And if you know someone facing their own first defence alone, go and stand with them.

For worship. He was deserted before we were. In Gethsemane his friends slept; in the courtyard Peter swore he did not know him; at the cross he cried that his God had forsaken him. He stood alone so that no believer ever need stand alone, and now he stands beside his servants in every courtroom, every hospital, every lonely room. To him be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.note: The “first defense” was a preliminary hearing at his trial.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus. Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Prisca and Aquila. The last words we have from Paul are greetings. Prisca and Aquila are the husband-and-wife team he met in Corinth when they had been expelled from Rome: tentmakers like himself, who worked with him in Corinth and Ephesus, took Apollos aside and explained the way of God more accurately, and once risked their necks for his life (Acts 18:2–3, 18, 26; Romans 16:3–4; 1 Corinthians 16:19). Many years of friendship lie behind the name. Prisca (Priscilla) is often named first, here as in Romans 16:3, perhaps because of her prominence in ministry or social standing. They were probably back in Ephesus. Paul also greets the household of Onesiphorus, the man who searched Rome until he found him (1:16–18); he greets the household rather than the man, which many take to mean he had since died.

I left Trophimus, who was ill. Erastus is possibly the city treasurer of Corinth (Romans 16:23), or the Erastus who served with Timothy (Acts 19:22). Trophimus was a Gentile from Ephesus who travelled with Paul (Acts 20:4; 21:29), and this small note is quietly significant. Paul, through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12; 28:8–9), did not heal him, and left him behind, too ill to travel. The gift of healing in the apostles was not at their command for every case; it served God’s purpose of confirming the gospel (Hebrews 2:3–4).

Do your best to come before winter. Winter closed the Mediterranean to shipping from about November to March, so Timothy had to travel before then or wait months. If he waited, he might arrive too late, and Paul did not expect to be alive. Behind the practical instruction is a man counting weeks. Tradition says Paul was executed soon after. We do not know whether Timothy made it.

Eubulus sends greetings. Four names we meet nowhere else in Scripture: Roman believers, keeping company with a condemned man when Demas would not. Linus is named by early church writers (Irenaeus) as the first leader of the church at Rome after the apostles. So the letter that records the desertion of Asia and of Demas ends with a short list of people who stayed.

The Lord be with your spirit. Then the final line, the last sentence of Paul’s that we possess. The first half is singular: “your” is to Timothy personally, the young man told to fan the fire into flame. And it is the handing over of a friendship. Paul will soon be taken from Timothy and may never see him again, so he commits him to the one companion who cannot be taken. The Lord who stood by Paul when everyone left (v. 17) is asked now to stand by Timothy. It is the promise of the risen Christ to all his servants: I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). Apostles die; the Lord of the apostles stays with his church.

Grace be with you. The second half is plural: grace be with you all, to the whole church. At the very end he turns from his friend to the whole room, as he did at the close of the first letter. The last written word of the apostle to the Gentiles is grace. After the shipwrecks and the floggings, the churches and the arguments, the deposit guarded and handed on, the desertions and the cloak left at Troas: grace. It is the word on which nearly all his letters close, and it is the right one.

Where Christians differ: does Linus show papal succession? Roman Catholic tradition lists Linus as the second pope after Peter, as evidence of an unbroken papal succession. Verdict: Paul mentions Linus only as one Roman believer among others, without any title. Early lists name him as a leader of the Roman church, but the New Testament knows nothing of a single bishop ruling the universal church. Churches were led by a plurality of elders. Christ alone is head of the church (Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18), and apostolic succession is succession in apostolic teaching.

What it does not mean. Trophimus’s illness does not mean he lacked faith, or that God does not heal today. God still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills (James 5:14–15). But the apostolic sign gifts were not permanent possessions to be used at will, and they ceased with the apostolic era. This commentary holds that cessationist view because Scripture ties the signs to the apostles and the founding of the church (2 Corinthians 12:12; Ephesians 2:20); many faithful Christians believe such gifts continue, and they too pray for the sick in faith.

We prayed for someone to be healed and they were not. Did we fail? No. Paul prayed and Trophimus stayed ill; Paul prayed three times about his own thorn and it stayed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). God is not a machine that heals when enough faith is inserted. He heals as he wills, sometimes by medicine, sometimes beyond it, sometimes not in this life, and the final healing of every believer is the resurrection. Keep praying, as James tells us; call the elders, and use doctors gratefully. When healing does not come, God is still good, and his grace is still sufficient. Anyone who tells a sick believer that he is ill because his faith is weak has not read this verse.

Why are all these names in the Bible? Because the gospel is carried by people, and God remembers them. These greetings show the church as it really was: a family of named individuals, couples, households, the sick and the faithful, men and women, many of whom we know nothing else about. They remind us that ministry is relationships, that Paul, for all his greatness, depended on friends, and that God keeps a record of every faithful believer, even those history forgets. Your name may never be in a book. It is written in a better one (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3).

On a Tuesday. If there is something you need to do before winter, a visit, a reconciliation, a word of thanks to someone who may not be here in spring, do it now.
verseByVerse.note: Winter closed the Mediterranean to shipping, so Timothy had to sail before it. Paul had healed others, yet left Trophimus ill.
